organisation_name_alt: Multiplant International Medicinal Conservation seed bank
overview_statement:
Multiplant International Medicinal Conservation/seed bank/arboretum (MIMC) is a non-profit making organization. MIMC is primarily concerned with wild plants conservation as well as integrating conservation with sustainable development, equitable use of aromatic and medicinal plants for the well-being of our entire society in general. The organization has put medicinal and aromatic plants to the economic benefits of disadvantaged people and especially the women to enhance gender equality and improve income in rural poor. The Specific objectives of MIMC are; 1. To undertake and encourage the planting and tending of valuable and endangered plant species. 2. To identify medicinal and aromatic plants species for which demand exist and which are suitable for cultivation in tropical countries. 3. To identify suitable partners among those who are cultivating land and forging alliances with interested individuals, particularly women, on alternative land use for the cultivation of medicinal and aromatic plants. 4. To carry out field trials with selected plants species. 5. To establish broad ranged field extraction facilities in rural areas. 6. To train people and particularly women in operating and maintaining field extraction facilities. 7. To set up a simple packaging and storage facilities for semi processed materials. 8. To establish in close collaboration with academic and research institutions on quality control mechanisms. 9. To encourage small-scale entrepreneurship and establish marketing mechanisms. 10. To liaise with similar initiatives elsewhere in tropical countries. 11. To mobilize funding from national, and international bodies to enable launching of the initiative and maintaining its functions Mimc activities; Since its inception, Mimc has advocated the establishment of medicinal plant nurseries in rural communities where useful plants are propagated and not only to provide a source of coveted medicinal and edible plants, but the purpose is to familiarize the public and especially the young people on useful medicinal plants that are used by their society in health improvement. We have established an ethnobotanic garden consisting of herbal indigenous plants which are in cultivated plots thus serving as demonstration and commercial garden whereby, over harvested wild plant species are planted. Activities at MIMC: • Propagation and cultivating of endangered medicinal plants • Medicinal plant nursery with over 100,000 seedlings. • Processing and packaging of medicinal plants • Environmental education and awareness creation • Vermiculture The Director, Mr. Joannes Bosco B. Samikwo, is also a herbal practitioner, and medicinal plants consultant in various organizations in Kenya. MIMC is accredited member of BGCI in the international agenda in plant conservation, also Mimc is accredited arboretum. One of the aims of BGCI is to ensure that national botanic gardens conserve indigenous flora. MULTIPLANT INTERNATIONAL MEDICINAL CONSERVATION Multiplant international medicinal conservation was founded in September 2002 with a mission of restoring, researching, capacity building and awareness creation on the uses of medicinal herbal plants for our own well-being, and conservation of indigenous wild plants species. And MIMC remains committed to supporting public rights to truthful information about the health benefit of medicinal herbal plants. With the little income Mimc generates from medicinal plants and products sale, Mimc has been able to undertake and perform some activities like; Monthly environmental and ethnobotanic education, putting medicinal plants to the economic benefits of disadvantaged communities to provide income, nutrition and health improvement. Mimc has also encouraged communities to plant valuable endangered medicinal plants like Artemisia afra, Justicia betonica, Echinops, Warburgia, Euphorbia crotonoides, Withania somnifera e.t.c as any other crop for their own benefit and the entire world community in the coming future. Through our education programmes, we are reaching about 300 people every month with accurate information on the safe and appropriate use of medicinal herbal plants. Environmental & Plant Conservation; Plants are important and yet their habitats are vitally important as well, plants provide us with; food, medicine, firewood, clothes, regulate climate, stabilizes the soil, oxygen production and it makes life on earth possible for both humans and all other animal form. The consumption of plant based medicines and health food is a worldwide phenomenon. This has resulted in the rapid growth in trade in hundreds of wild crafted and cultivated medicinal plants and development of a sophisticated botanical extraction industry. Plant species are vanishing at an alarming rate, and out of 270,000 of the plant species found in 200 countries, one in eight is threatened with extinction. And this is brought up by the loss of wild habitats, growing industrialization, urbanization, intensive farming and unsustainable harvesting of wild species and ideally, together we can save plant live before being destructed or over harvested. Sustainable management of traditional medicinal plants resources is important, not only because of their value as a potential source of new drugs but due to reliance on traditional medicinal plants for health. The vast majority of people in Africa consult traditional medicinal practitioners for their health care. With few exceptions, traditional medicinal plants are gathered from the wild. Although reliance on traditional medicinal practitioners may decline in long term as alternative health care, facilities become available, increasing demand for popular herbal medicines is expected in the foreseeable future. Over the same period, certain vegetation types that were sources of supply of traditional medicines are drastically vanishing due to forest clearance for agriculture, uncontrolled burning, logging and livestock grazing. And exclusion from core conservation areas adversely affects traditional medicinal practitioners who previously gathered medicinal plants in those sites. In addition, supplies of herbal medicines to traditional medicinal practitioners are affected by competing resource use such as; timber logging, commercial harvesting for export etc. This creates a growing demand for fewer resources in some cases resulting in local disappearance of favored and effective sources of traditional medicine and reduced species diversity. The most vulnerable species are popular, slow growing or slow to reproduce or species with specific habitat requirements and a limited distribution. Although in theory, sustainable use of bark, roots or whole plant used as herbal medicines is possible, the high levels of money and manpower for intensive management of slow growing species in multiple species systems are unlikely to be found in most African countries. The cultivation of alternative sources of supply of popular, high conservation areas is therefore essential. However, commercial cultivation of such species is not a simple solution and at present, it is unlikely to be profitable due to the slow growth rate for most species and low prices paid for traditional medicines. With over 1200 species of indigenous plants growing in our Ethnobotanic garden, the garden is becoming a seed bank of many species that are locally, nationally or internationally threatened. Environmental education MIMC runs courses on herbal medicines, plant identification, tree growing and management (from tree nursery to forest establishment) and nature walks. For bookings, contact Joannes on 0735393606; email: samikwo@gmail.com MIMC ASSOCIATED ACTIVITIES Since its establishment in the year 2002, we started with a small home tree nursery that consisted of 1 tree species (Pittosporum viridiflorum) and gradually, the tree nursery begun to emerge and so far we’ve planted over 500,000 seedlings since we started. MIMC plant collection, propagation and conservation activities MIMC has collected, conserved, propagated and planted over 6,500 species of trees, shrubs, lianas and herbs since September 2002. These can be found both inside the main garden tree nursery, also seedlings can be obtained from our extension tree nurseries and retail outlets countrywide and across East Africa. Multiplant medicinal nursery currently has many species for sale, especially on contract order. We mainly concentrate on unusual indigenous trees and non tree plants found in local habitat.

overview_statement: The plot was purchased in 1992. The overall size is 25 acres and was owned by a Swahili family from Malindi. Historically, these parcels of land were the country farms for wealthy families situated in Malindi, growing cashew nut, coconut, maize, as well as an assortment of other livestock and subsistence produce. The farm was in a state of neglect when it was purchased, which meant the maize fields, which covered over 70% of the land, had grown back. The native rootstock from previous slash and burn remained alive and had regrown. It was with little thought that we allowed this bush to remain and we encouraged the bush to thrive as it was a habitat for many of the indigenous fauna and flora. Our main interest was the areas of coconut and cashew nut plantation, where we established a high intensive nursery specifically growing ornamental exotic species for the local market. Our joy of indigenous trees meant that we added indigenous trees that we had collected from all corners of Kenya. Our business has flourished and the use of the land has simply become more and more intensive. Knowing this, not once have we applied pressure to develop areas of the indigenous bush, as it is in our interest in enhancing the wild areas as not only are they beautiful but they provide a wonderful seed bank. Gede has now become a miniature forest and is an island surrounded by destroyed landscapes. We have been very fortunate that a reliable source of potable water, albeit expensive, is close at hand. This source of water is becoming less and less dependable and more and more expensive. Pressure from the local cities, such as Malindi and Mombasa, mean that the price of water is becoming unaffordable. This has meant a shift in the species of plants that we target. Indigenous is increasingly suitable and the future lies in changing our overall plant selection and number of species to be a 25% exotic, 75% indigenous mix by 2025.

organisation_name: Gareev Botanical Garden of NAS KR
overview_statement:
The Gareev Botanical Garden of National Academy of Sciences of the Kyrgyz Republic was established in 1938 and is a centre for the research and conservation of the biodiversity of local and foreign flora. It is a leading research institution in the field of introduction and acclimatisation, physiology, selection and genetics of plants. The botanical garden has a unique collection which numbers nearly 5000 taxa of higher vascular plants. The Botanical Garden is located in Bishkek, in the foothills area of the Chui Valley at about 900 meters altitude. The total area is 150 hectares. 

From 2009 as part of a Darwin Initiative-funded project (2009 – 2012) on participative forest management in the Tian-Shan region of Kyrgyzstan, Gareev Botanical Garden has been working with Botanic Gardens Conservation International (BGCI) to create a panel exhibition containing information on key species of Kyrgyzstan’s fruit and nut forests. The botanic garden provides an ideal vehicle to publicise the conservation work of the project and reach out to a large public regarding the importance of the wild fruit and nut forests of Kyrgyzstan. Many of the species that have been researched under this Darwin Initiative, grow in the garden’s living collections offering thereby an excellent opportunity to visualise these species live supported by special displays and plant labels.

overview_statement:
Tromsø Arctic-Alpine Botanic Garden (TAABG) is a unit at The Arctic University Museum of Norway. Officially opened in 1994, it became the world’s northernmost botanic garden. The location is at the main campus of the UIT The Arctic University of Norway, formerly known as the University of Tromsø.

The Garden occupies an area of about 1.6 hectares, mainly consisting of rock and crevice garden landscapes. It is situated in a gently sloping landscape between a natural birch forest and the harbour. It is divided into 27 sections, partly according to plant families or geographical origin, and partly as special topics. The largest and best developed collections are known under the following names: the Himalayas, the Arctic, Gentianaceae, Primulaceae, Saxifragaceae, South America, and the North-Norwegian Traditional Garden plants. The herb garden is also very popular. Continuous improvements of the rock landscape have given a wider range of habitats in several collections, including Africa, the Arctic, Caucasus, Gentianaceae, New Zealand, Saxifragaceae, and South America. The Garden has a small cafeteria located in a traditional 19th Century private resident building.

The cafeteria is open from ca. 1st of June to the end of August. During summer, the Garden is open 24 hours and is admission is free. During the snow season (ca. October to April), the garden is closed. It is possible to book guided tours for a fee for groups of 10 persons or more. We encourage horticulturists and botanists who plan to visit the garden to contact staff a few weeks before arrival.
mission_statement:
Tromsø Arctic-Alpine Botanic Garden (TAABG) is a public garden with cultural, scientific and educational tasks and missions, which include:

·         Maintenance of scientific plant collections containing well-documented and properly labelled plant material.

·         Research, testing, and plant cultivation, with particular focus on taxa that can be grown at high northern latitudes.

·         Contribution to ex-situ conservation of plants that are threatened in nature, including species from Norway and other cool biomes of the world.

·         On-site education to students and children at all levels (university, high school, elementary school, and kindergarten), and to the general public, on plants, natural and cultural history, gardening, northern climates, and conservation biology.

·         Public outreach to the wider public using a variety of techniques and outreach platforms, including oral, written and audiovisual dissemination.

overview_statement:
The Botanical Garden and Herbarium (BG&H) department of Botany at University of Malakand, Chakdara Dir (L.) Khyber puthtunkhwa, Pakistan launched in 2006 by Higher Education Commission (HEC) of Pakistan and registered with the Botanical Garden Conservation International in 2014. In the botanical garden, 7 thousand herbs, shrubs and trees are growing tolerable. They have economical, medicinal and ethno-botanical application cited in different literature. The garden has been properly looked after and retained fine. The garden is well equipped with lath houses and glass house. Several representative small gardens like, Quranic garden, Olive garden, Jasmine garden, Punica garden, Cacti garden and Rose garden have already been installed.       
 Herbarium is a collection of pressed and dried plant specimens mounted on herbarium sheets. About 2000 dry plant specimens are also preserved in the herbarium under proper defined protocols collected from different localities of Malakand division. More than 60% plants are endemic to Malakand division, and fully acclimatized with the environmental condition of botanical garden and herbarium. 
Different approaches have been tested for domestication of the endangered and medicinally important flora of Khyber Pakhtunkhwa. In this connection different pilot project has been started/completed/running with collaborators, like Caralluma, Olea, Phaseolus, Pisum, Cicer, Ricinus, Nigella and Brassica etc.

organisation_name: Hervey Bay Botanic Gardens (Great Sandy Region Botanic Gardens)
System Garden - The University of Melbourne
overview_statement:
The System Garden is a unique scientific, cultural and landscape feature of the University of Melbourne’s Parkville campus, which is situated on Wurundjeri land. Prior to the colonial settlement of Melbourne in 1835, the area the System Garden is situated on was grassy woodland plains dominated by River Red Gum (Eucalyptus camaldulensis), over a rich grass layer of mainly Kangaroo Grass (Themeda triandra), occurring on fertile clays.

The System Garden was established in 1856, by the university’s first professor of Natural Sciences, Frederick McCoy, who wanted a useful scientific garden which enabled the active and passive teaching of botany, suitable for a community of scholars and educators.

Its original circular format, with a conservatory in the centre, was laid out by Edward La Trobe Bateman, who designed the university’s campus and other significant gardens in Melbourne.   

The System Garden is now both, a public ornamental garden and a teaching garden. It is configured specifically to show the evolutionary relationships between plants. Starting off with algae, mosses, ferns, in the fernery, moving through to an interesting collection of cycads then onto the gymnosperms, progressing through to the 11 different subclasses of the flowering plants (angiosperms). The angiosperms are arranged according to the Cronquist system of plant classification.

There are other noteworthy sections of the garden that are not part of the formal systematic layout which include the award-winning Australian rainforest, which features ferns, palms and epiphytic plants; the Apothecary Garden with a fine espalier Ginkgo biloba and other medicinal plants and a Pollinator Garden, with a selection of nectar and pollen producing plants to support the unique insect hotel and chimney beehive.

The garden also features a number of rare and unusual specimen trees, some of which are registered on the National Trust Significant Tree Register and the City of Melbourne Exceptional Tree Register.

 The System Garden serves not only as a living laboratory, but also contributes to school and community education and recreation for all ages.

It is open to the public Monday to Friday 8.00am to 5.00pm. Closed on the weekend.

Entrance is free.

overview_statement:
The Project of Ushuaia's Botanic Garden started in 2018 when non-profit NGO Asociación Nuria Tierra del Fuego signed an agreement with the local municipality, and was thereby granted the use and custody of a 10-hectare patch of native forest, a few kilometers from the center of Ushuaia.

Asociación Nuria TDF is carrying out a 10-year- Conservation Plan for the Nothofagus native forest in the Botanic Garden, with state funds. Some actions performed with these funds are:

The interpretation trail

A list of the species present in the BG

Work with the community: replanting trees in several areas of the city of Ushuaia.

Visits to the BG once a month for the general public and a full program of school visits throughout the year

In addition, there is another project in the process: The Forest Library.

The Forest Library includes:

The creation of a web page that will house a digital library about the species present in the BG,

An embroidered library of the species: Fifty species are being embroidered to be exhibited at the Botanic Garden's tea house.

Our next tasks are:

To establish our collections policy (until now we've worked on our in situ collection, the native forest area)

To create a governance structure
mission_statement: To protect, grow and exhibit the plant diversity of the region, through the conservation of endemic and endangered species; creating bonds with the local communities and visitors from around the world. To generate exchanges with the local scientific community, at national and international levels, to develop interpretation, research, education, recreation, tourist and social activities, withing a sustainable framework.

overview_statement:
In the Botanical Garden we find the following plots:

- 2,5 acres arboretum in which the trees and bushes are systematically arranged 
- 1000 square meters of herbs and poisonous plants, classified according to phytochemical principles
- 129 square meters taste and touch garden where the plants are labelled in Braille.
- 2000 square meters alpine garden arranged according to geographical and geological principles including plants from all over the globe.
- 80 square meters Alpine House
- 1000 square meters   systematic garden, an area in which the plants are arranged according to plant families

633 m2 tropical greenhouse: tropical houseplants, water plants, ferns, epiphytes, carnivorous plants, cacti and succulents, plants from the Mediterranean and the Canary Islands.
Opening Hours:
The park and all other open-air grounds are open throughout the year from 7.30 to 19.00 (to 16.30 during the winter months). No entrance fees. The tropical green houses are open every Tuesday,Thursday and every first Sunday in the month from 13.00 to 16.00

overview_statement:
The Antwerp Botanic Garden is a green oasis in the busy centre of Antwerp.

In the Garden you can find a substantial number of exceptional trees and shrubs. The herbal collection contains about 2.000 pieces, among which several are legally protected. In the greenhouse is a large collection of tropical and subtropical species.

The Garden has a history of more than 200 years. In the early years it was the medical garden of the nearby Saint Elisabeth hospital. About 125 years ago, important botanical and scientific research was done here. Since 1926, the garden is under the administration of the city council. In 1950, the garden was classified als a landscape of great value.

overview_statement:
The park is situated in Waasland approximately 10 km outside Antwerp. It has a typical romantic design with alternating large tree clusters, lawns and water features. The castle ruin (1790), visible from various sites, dominates the landscape. Renovation of the castle started in september 2004. The total area is more than 24 ha of which 13 form the arboretum; the remaining grounds comprise a nature garden, fruit orchard, agricultural field and a little brook. The arboretum was founded by the Decalut family in 1980. Nowadays the arboretum is managed by the commune of Beveren.

It now comprises more than 4500 plants including 70 Quercus spp., varieties and cultivars, more than 62 Ilex spp., 88 Viburnum spp., and 54 Cornus spp.. The soil belongs to the Fago-quercetum association which is perfect for oak, beech, chestnut, European aspen, birch, honeysuckle, rowan, hazel-nut, bird-cherry and holly. The focus of the park is on educating the broad public with respect to flora and the natural environment. The most striking trees in the collection are the giant copper beeches.Some of them had to be cut down in january 2006 because of parasits (fungi). Some eye-catching rare species include Betula medwediewii, Betula papyrifera or Betula turkestanica (2 m dwarf form). Also of note are a gigantic Thuja plicata, an old white mulberry, Ailanthus vilmoriniana, a deep purple Magnolia liliflora Nigra, and an old Catalpa bignonioides amongst others.

The arboretum is bordered by a small forest dominated by chestnut trees with accompanying undergrowth shrubs, herbaceous plants and ferns. In this part we find an old ice-house that is presently a shelter for bats. Another attraction of the park is its wealth of birds. Guided tours are organised on request on the opening days. A small information folder is available, educational brochures, exhibitions and various other activities are regularly organised.

overview_statement:
The Jardin Botanico VerdeNativo is located 5 min drive from the village of Puerto Octay, in the beautiful countryside of the Chilean Lake District (X Región de Los Lagos) in the heart of the Temperate Rainforest in southern Chile. Its origins date back to 1998, thanks to the dedication of its founder, the Chilean-Croatian businessman from the city of Antofagasta (northern Chile), Anton Ilijic Richards.

The 20 hectares of land are a haven of lush biodiversity, housing an astonishing variety of over 700 species of Chilean native plants from all over the country, including 50% of all Chilean threatened plants, as well as plants from the Juan Fernández Archipelago.

The current botanical collections are grouped into three distinct (albeit overlapping) categories: taxonomic collections (Nothofagus, Chilean and introduced conifers, Myrtaceae, Azara and Berberis, among many others); geographic collections (Juan Fernández, Central Chile); and ecological collections (relict of Valdivian Temperate Rainforest).

The garden features an attractive network of paths and its botanical collections are labelled with identification labels that follow the standards of Botanic Garden Conservation International (BGCI) and the Royal Botanic Garden’s Kew.
mission_statement: To conserve and promote the biological diversity of plant species in a restored habitat in southern Chile, establishing links with national and international institutions for scientific research, conservation and safeguarding activities for native and endemic species of the country, also promoting environmental education and community outreach for a better understanding of the natural environment and the importance of conserving and preserving our plant heritage. From scientific activities to educational programs and specialized tourism, Jardin Botánico VerdeNativo is a benchmark in conservation, education and recreation.

organisation_name_alt: Botanická zahrada Přírodovědecké fakulty Univerzity Karlovy
overview_statement:
The Botanical Garden of the Faculty of Science of Prague’s Charles University (Botanical Garden CU) covers an area of 3.5 ha. In the complex there is a building of the Department of Botany of Charles University Faculty of Science, another belonging to the Institute for Environmental Studies and also the Department of Education and Student Affairs of the Faculty of Science. The public area is divided into the greenhouses and outdoor sections. The greenhouses are home to a permanent exhibition from the tropics and dry subtropics (the cacti and succulent collection). In the summer the collection of plants from the wet subtropics is installed outdoors according to their continents of origin; in winter the plants are stored in a large cold greenhouse. In addition to the extensive collection of succulents, noteworthy are the large and old specimens of cycads, camellias, myrtles and other plants from the collections of the former 19th century Smíchov university gardens. Important in the outdoor exhibition is a unique specimen of Ginkgo biloba, Ginkgo biloba cv. Praga, initially shaped using bonsai techniques, estimated to be about 130 years old, as well as one of the first dawn redwoods introduced into Europe, and other trees. The most valuable exhibition is a collection of Central European flora, founded in 1904 and maintained continuously ever since.

The collection is visited annually by about 100 000 people. It serves not only as a source of demonstration material for students of biology and related fields from both Charles University and its affiliated colleges and secondary schools, but also contributes to community education and recreation for all ages, especially for the people of Prague 2.
mission_statement:
The main functions are connected to the Charles University, Faculty of Science:

  • Research infrastructure

  • Space for protection of biodiversity and collection work

  • Space for education, interpretation of the research done at the Faculty of Sciences and public relations

  • Infrastructure for University education

  • Park enclave of the University campus

overview_statement:
The Freiburg-Günterstal Arboretum has been set up in the Municipal Forest District of Freiburg - Günterstal Forest Range - in cooperation with the Forest Faculty of the Albert-Ludwig-University of Freiburg and its Botanical Garden.

For the specialist:  
The Arboretum is a spot of supplementary education: proving and enhancing knowledge of family order, generic term or species of trees and shrubs; determining them and becoming acquainted with them; gathering illustrative material; verifying economical usability and suitability for landscape architecture. It is supposed to help maintain and develop tree species endangered at their natural stands.  

For the uninitiated:  
The Arboretum is - as for a globetrotter - an opportunity to learn about trees and shrubs of other continents and countries. People interested in dendrology, forestry or horticulture meet new and versatile forest aspects that contribute to the diversity of forests and to the enrichment of landscapes. For native but so far unnoticed or mostly ignored tree and shrub species, e.g. Yew or Service Tree the Arboretum should be conducive.  
Tree species diversity of comparable geographical latitudes is strikingly higher in America or Eastern Asia than in Europe. The reason for this was the evasive movement of tree species during the Ice Age and their later remigration. On the European Continent remigration was - because of the East-West-extension of the Alps - either infeasible or possible only on a small scale. Many tree species that are going to be reintroduced today had been native before the Ice Age Period, e.g. Big Tree (Sequoiadendron giganteum), Red Cedar (Thuja plicata), Yellow Poplar (Liriodendron tulipifera) and others. From this point of view, reintroducing does not mean cultivating "foreign tree species" but the return of former native species. This is what the Arboretum wants to contribute to.

overview_statement: The Arboretum of Szarvas is Hungary's largest arboretum: 82 hectares, of which 62 hectares are open to visitors. 45 hectares are a nature reserved and a living gene bank. The gene bank collection consists of 327 taxa 983 specimens, including an evergreen collection of 91 taxa 651 specimens. It is an English garden style arboretum and its main value is its spatial structure, with a balanced composition of evergreen and deciduous species. The central core is the Pepikert, a garden created by Count Paul Bolza in the late 1800s. It is a popular destination for visiting tourists.

overview_statement: The Hungarian University of Agriculture and Life Sciences Gödöllő Botanical Garden was founded in 1959 as the First Agrobotanical Garden of Hungary. The Collection of Cultivated plants is one of the most emphasized part of the garden. Beside numerous species of the Hungarian Flora visitors can get acquainted with several indigenous species of faraway continents. Out of the 15 main thematic collections of the garden, the Lily tree Collection, the Wild rose Collection and the Bamboo Collection are also outstanding on a national level. The botanical garden is a nature conservation area with regard to the relict forest stand of `Aceri campestri-Quercetum roboris`. Botanical Garden homes about 1.8 thousand plant species, and the number of protected plant species from the Hungarian Flora more than 100.

overview_statement:
Ahalia campus lying in the eastern part of the Palakkad gap of western ghats experiences slightly semi-arid conditions and the land scape looks mostly dry for most part of the year. The district though rich in bio-diversity has no single location where the bio resources is properly maintained as a germplasm. To fill the void and make the landscape greener, Ahalia foundation embarked on a remarkable programme christened Green Ahalia with the patronage of our visionary chairman Dr. Gopal who is passionate about the environment Conservation and Sustainable use. We began the journey from June 5, 2017 establishing thematic gardens.

Currently we have 36 themes that will touch 50 in a couple of years. Our stress is projecting and conserving bio resources, preserving a germplasm, promoting sustainable use. Towards achieving this goal we have been creating facilities for propagation, maintaining rich stock of planting materials, stocking of seeds and propagation materials and so on. These are achieved through the dedicated service of a small but passionate team committed to fostering environment. In our effort we could receive liberal support and guidance from various quarters which include institutes of excellence, NGOs, CBOs, Educational institutes, state government departments etc. to our luck we have the best brains to guide us by way of our Advisory Board Members. We are aiming high and trying to reach out. During the short period of our existence, we could make perceptible impact and achieve recognitions.

overview_statement: Malabar Botanical Garden, Kozhikode, Kerala State, India, located in the panoramic, serene suburban area of Calicut (Kozhikode) city (8 Km from Railway Station and 25 Km from Airport) is renowned for its excellent fresh water plant collections of India. The garden sprawls over 16 ha area with 6 ha wetland which transforms into a placid lake during monsoon, ideal for wetland flora conservation. The climate is tropical with 3000 mm annual rainfall, high humidity and short summer (Feb-May) with maximum temperature up to 320C. The wetland gradually elevates to a 45 m high lateritic hillock facilitating niche for a wide range of plants. The Malabar Botanical Garden has 8 green houses for primitive plants (mosses and ferns), shade loving plants, orchids, medicinal plants, aquatic plants, etc.) Malabar Botanical Garden is a centre of Research in Biodiversity conservation and related topics.

organisation_name: Sgrf Hortus Malabaricus Medicinal Plants Garden
overview_statement:
Kerala state of India is a small strip of land bordered to the east by the

Western Ghats and in the west by the Arabian sea. The northern part of

a land strip known during medieval period as the Malabar coast, is

blessed with an immense variety of flora and fauna including the famous

spices which attracted traders from the Arabian region and explorers

alike. The region was alternately controlled by the Portuguese, Dutch and

later the British, as their colony. It was during the Dutch period that,

realizing the scientific value of documenting the diversity of natural

resources, the monumental task of scientific exploration of the local

natural resources and their detailed documentation including ethnobotanical

and ethnohistorical knowledge of the natives, particularly their

medicinal uses, was undertaken, primarily directed by the then Dutch         

Governor of Cochin, Hendrik Adriaan van Rheede.

This colossal effort by a

large team of experts including physicians, scientists, artists, plant

collectors and interpreters of Malabar and Europe led to the earliest and

most important printed book on Indian plants in any European language,

namely the Hortus Malabaricus. The book consisted of 12 volumes

published starting from 1678 to 1693 from Amsterdam.

This pre-Linnaean monumental work contains 793 illustrations, describing

about 739 species of plants in 742 “chapters”. In Hortus Malabaricus,

the name of the plant in different languages is given followed by a short

description starting with habitat and ending with the medicinal properties

and method of administration. Information on plant names and their

medicinal uses were provided by the native physicians and four

renowned physicians were associated with van Rheede’s project: Itty

Achudan, Ranga Bhatt, Vinayaka Pandit and Apu Bhatt. These physicians

provided the plant names and certified their medical uses.

Hortus Malabaricus was translated from Latin into English in a monumental

35-year project that was led by eminent plant taxonomist Prof. K.

S. Manilal, Emeritus; Calicut University. The 12 volumes - van Rheede’s

Hortus Malabaricus (Malabar Garden) English edition with annotations

and Modern Botanical Nomenclature were published in 2003 by the

University of Kerala, Thiruvananthapuram.

 

Sgrf’s Hortus Malabaricus Medicinal Plants Garden

Though several studies have been carried out on the plants described in

Hortus Malabaricus, there have not been many successful efforts to

collect and conserve the plants described in it. A project on the collection

and ex-situ conservation of the medicinal plants described in van

Rheede’s Hortus Malabaricus was initiated at SGRF, Cheruthuruthy,

Shoranur, Kerala in 2016. During the last four years the collection of

plant species at SGRF have collected 709 references from

Hortus Malabaricus, which includes wild orchids, tubers, trees, herbs and

aquatic and semi-aquatic plants. Many plants in this important collection

are endemic and belong to the endangered category; several of them

have disappeared from their type localities as described by Van Rheede.

Our goal is to complete the collection in the next 1 years. In addition, the

garden has an orchidarium, pepper garden, banana garden and various other

plants that grow naturally in Kerala.
mission_statement:
1. Vision

Conservation and Study of Medicinal plants described in Hortus Malabaricus and plant diversity of the Western Ghats and Kerala. Provide a ‘living’ biobank of native species to enable genetic research.

 2. Mission

To transform a 25 acre estate at Nedumpura as a botanical garden through the cultivation, propagation and data collection of the medicinal plants, wild orchids, wild varieties of cultivated crops and native varieties of crops and interesting plant species. Conduct in-house research on selected plants and map traits to genetic variants.

organisation_name: Giardino Botanico Alpino alle Viote del M. Bondone
overview_statement:
Viote Alpine Botanical Garden is one of the oldest and largest alpine gardens in Italy and it has a focus on alpine species.

It was founded in the late 1930’s to promote environmental education and to contribute to the conservation of the alpine flora. Since its inception, the Garden was developed as part of Trento Science Museum, now MUSE, an extensive network of science and nature museums in Trentino, NE Italy. "Viote” is a well-know area for its unique grasslands that naturally host a very diverse flora, being the ideal setting for an alpine garden.

Located at an altitude of about 1500 meters above the sea level, the Botanical Garden faces south and is naturally rich in water, thanks to a neighbouring peat bog. Almost 1,000 species of alpine plants are currently cultivated in the Garden. They are native of the major mountains of the world. Medicinal plants and endangered native taxa are a special focus of the Garden.

Viote Alpine Botanical Garden contributes to biodiversity conservation growing, propagating and banking the seeds of endangered plants native of the Eastern Italian Alps. The central rock garden covers approximately 2 hectares and is surrounded by woods and meadows for other 8 hectares, where a nature trail guides the visitor through the most significant alpine habitats (flower-rich grasslands, forests, alpine shrubs and peat bogs). Other points of interest include arable fields with neglected and underutilized crops, a local vegetable garden, a viewpoint on the famous Dolomite massif Brenta Group, a sensory path, an area hosting temporary photographic exhibitions, an area dedicated to bees and additional information on plant adaptation at high altitude engaging the senses.

The Viote Botanical Garden envisages itself as an open-air museum, where the botanical part is included in its ecological complexity and space is also given to other disciplines. Indeed, every summer the Garden offers to its visitors a rich programme of entertaining and educational events. Among the others, various workshops, interactive guided tours, events, courses, exhibitions, tented experiences and concerts.

organisation_name_alt: Botanic Garden, Field Science Center for Northern Biosphere, Hokkaido University
overview_statement: Hokkaido University Botanic Garden, opened in 1886, occupies 13.3 hectares in the heart of Sapporo city and is a ten-minute walk from Sapporo station. The garden includes remnants of natural woodlands with old growth trees of Japanese elm, showing the original landscape of Sapporo before the urban development. It is home to a collection of around 4,000 plant taxa with a focus on alpine and cool-temperate plants in Hokkaido and neighboring areas. The garden offers beautiful botanical sights all year round and highlights include enchanting spring ephemeral wildflowers, Japanese cherry blossoms or sakura, and autumn leaves. Additionally, the museum built in 1882 exhibits old natural history specimens and items related to the colonization of Hokkaido, and Northern Peoples Museum displays artifacts describing the culture of people indigenous to Hokkaido.
mission_statement: The botanic garden is a facility of Hokkaido University for botanical research, education, and conservation, and also open to the public and contributes to public education and recreation.

overview_statement:
History

In 1915, a Forest Researcher Mr. Alex Rogers founded the Botanical Garden. He planned, chose, located, and established it as an international garden. Recently after the establishment of the garden, in 1917, Mr. Otway Wheeler Cuffe and his wife Mr. Charlotte Wheeler Cuffe helped Mr. Rogers with the ideas, formation, landscaping, and building the garden after London's Kew Gardens. Before it was only 150 acres in area.

On December 1st, 1924 the Botanical Garden was turned into the National Botanical Garden with a total of 240 acres. The garden was well preserved by the Ministry of Forestry. In 2000, the garden was renovated and now it has great landscaping and scenic view.

A tower was built in the National Kandawgyi Gardens on April 11th, 2002 and was opened on December 18th, 2003. The diameter of the tower is 50 feet and has a height of 215 feet. There are 12 levels, where 10 levels are for viewing the beautiful scenes of the garden. And 11th floor is a Function Hall.

Garden Highlights

Orchid Garden, Children Playground, Pagoda Island, Tea House, Souvenir Center, Cascadean Garden, Rainbow Fountain, Swamp Walkway, Rock Garden, Bamboo Garden, Croton Garden, Pine Forest, Timber Walkways, Rain Forest, Walk in Aviary and Takin Compound are other interesting places to visit in National Kandawgyi Gardens.

Objectives

- To serve as a recreation center for the public.
- To carry out educational activities related to conservation of trees and forests so that people will become interested and appreciate the values of trees and flowers.
- To assist botanists and researchers with their studies.
- To collect and reproduce rare and endangered plant species for their perpetual existence, conduct research activities and assist the development of ecotourism industry.

mission_statement: The Vasile Fati Botanical Garden is dedicated to the conservation and sustainable use of plant diversity through ex situ and in situ programs, innovative scientific research, and public education. As a living laboratory and cultural landmark of Transylvania, the Garden advances the understanding the impact of climate change on plants, safeguards native and endangered species, and promotes ecological awareness. We are committed to fostering international collaboration, inspiring communities, and ensuring that Romania’s botanical heritage continues to thrive for future generations.

organisation_name: Botanical Garden of Tver State University
overview_statement:
The Botanic Garden of Tver State University is situated at the meeting place of the Volga and Tvertza rivers. It is one of the main green spaces of Tver. Many centuries ago the territory of the Garden belonged to Otroch monastery - the oldest settlement of the town of Tver. The area was occupied by Zavolzhsky trading quarter. The history of the garden goes back to 1879 when Ilia Ivanovich Bobrov, a merchant of the first guild, an honary citizen of the town, planted a small private garden. Some of the trees planted at that time have been preserved till now. Subsequently the garden passed into the hands of Leonid Antonovich Kolakovsky, a teacher of Sciences of Tver State Modern School. He managed to accumulate a rather interesting collection of tree and shrub species at the small territory of 1,5 ha.
 After the October Revolution the garden passed under charge of municipal department of public education and was used as a leisure activity center for children. In 1939 the Garden was affiliated to the Pedagogical Institute. The main planting occured between 1939 and 1941 but a great number of plants disappeared during Word War. 
   Since 1949 the garden had been reconstructed according to the programme developed by M.L.Nevsky. The programme was centered around educational issues and popularization of plant introduction and acclimatization experiments. 
   In 1971 Tver State University, the former Pedagogical Institute, refused to support the garden and the garden passed to municipal plant-growing holding. The smaller part of the living collections was moved to the agro-biological station of Tver State University. In the 1970s and 1980s the garden was neglected. Research and educational activities were not performed and the garden became a recreation center. The largest part of the living collections perished, only few tree specimens were preserved. There were only 3 members on staff and no wonder the garden was not properly tended to. 
   Since 1989 the Botanical Garden has been affiliated to Tver State University. The work on the reconstruction of the garden and its collections and development of new living collections has been carried out first under the directorship of K.M.Smirnova, then under the guidance of A.P.Khokhryakov and M.T.Mazurenko. 
   In the course of its long history the Botanic Garden of Tver State University has developed into a unique institution valuable for science, culture and leisure. It is the only Botanic Garden in the upper reaches of the Volga River. 
   The Botanic Garden has the sectors of "Dendrology", "Wild Flora", "Ornamental Flower Gardening" and "Herbarium". At present the Botanic Garden of Tver State University has a collection of 350 species of trees and shrubs and 2 000 species of herbaceous plants. 
   Plants grown in the open air are distributed according to natural ecological zones: the Far East, Europe and North America. The Botanic Garden has a number of floristic exhibitions.

overview_statement:
HISTORIQUE
Ce Jardin d’Expérimentation des Plantes Utiles (JEPU) du Laboratoire de Pharmacognosie et Botanique (UCAD/Faculté de Médecine et Pharmacie) est créé en 1986; surface d’environ 1,9 ha; objectifs: enseignement de la botanique appliquée (plantes utiles), multiplication et production de graines, recherche; personnel: 1 conservateur et 2 jardiniers autrefois rémunérés par ENDA-Tiers Monde; locaux (bureau, stockage de semences, outillage) incendiés en 2002 et non restaurés; équipements (pépinière, ombrière, case d'exposition) hors d'état; l'herbier est à reconstituer.  

Les activités du JEPU sont concentrées autour de la culture et de la présentation d’espèces utiles d'Afrique de l'Ouest, sur la conservation de ces espèces, ainsi que sur la multiplication et la production de plants pour les opérations de reboisement (environ 400 espèces). Il apparaît clairement que les objectifs, auxquels aspire ce jardin membre des JBF, ne peuvent être réalisés avec les moyens actuels. Les projets sur la Biodiversité végétale: BGCI, FSP, PGIES, AFORNET, UICN etc... devront aider à résoudre ce problème, en complément des ressources de l’UCAD.

Dans le cadre du projet IEC/PM, notre jardin dispose, dorénavant, de cinq (5) sites de démonstration (Carrés Botaniques Villageois) à Keur Goury, Mbadakhoune, Sambandé, Kaymor et Diakhao, (Sine Saloum); Sites dans lesquels les chercheurs du JEPU mènent des expériences de conservation de plantes médicinales, en partenariat avec ENDA et PROMETRA (ONG). Quelques moyens logistiques sont nécessaires au JEPU pour parfaire ces relations. 
 
ACTIVITES DU JEPU
La conservation «ex-situ» est reconnue comme l’un des outils les plus importants, que les jardins botaniques peuvent mettre en place dans la conservation de la biodiversité.

The Botanics Gardens Conservation Strategy établit que «Le but de la conservation ex situ est de fournir une "réserve" pour la protection. Ceci ne se justifie que comme un des éléments d’une stratégie globale de conservation qui, à terme, assure une survie des espèces dans la nature. Son rôle devrait être perçu comme un moyen d’atteindre un objectif et non comme un objectif en lui-même: comme une source de matériaux pour la réintroduction dans des habitats dégradés et pour renforcer des populations dans des programmes de gestion des écosystèmes, pour la recherche et l’éducation, pour sélectionner du matériel végétal à des fins commerciales dans des pépinières, l’agriculture locale, les plantations d’agréments, la sylviculture locale, etc... Un autre rôle est de soustraire les populations d'espèces sauvages aux pressions des scientifiques, des horticulteurs, des amateurs ou des collectionneurs locaux. Par dessus tout, la conservation ex-situ rend les plantes disponibles pour l’exploitation humaine (IUCN-BGCS et WWF 1989, p. 21)».

La conservation ex-situ a plusieurs objectifs:
 	Sauvegarder des ressources génétiques menacées.
 	Fournir le matériel végétal pour la réintroduction, le renforcement, la restauration des habitats et leur gestion.
 	Fournir du matériel pour la recherche biologique sur la conservation.
 	Centraliser du matériel végétal sous formes variées pour constituer des banques de gènes.
 	Fournir du matériel végétal afin de supprimer ou de réduire la pression provenant de la collecte sauvage.
 	Cultiver des espèces à semences récalcitrantes qui ne peuvent être maintenues dans des banques de graines.
 	Rendre disponible du matériel pour les expositions et l’éducation au sujet de la conservation.

La conservation ex-situ des plantes sauvages est un rôle unique et central des jardins botaniques. Ils possèdent les installations appropriées et le personnel compétent en botanique et en horticulture pour être «la police d’assurance» contre l’extinction des végétaux. La conservation ex-situ peut inclure le maintien d’échantillons de populations, aussi bien que les graines, le pollen, les propagules, la culture cellulaire et tissulaire.

Comme méthode de conservation, la conservation ex-situ est de façon inhérente déficiente dans le fait qu’il n’est pas toujours possible de maintenir plus d’un échantillon limité de la diversité génétique, en culture ou en banque. De plus, cela peut mener à un changement génétique imprévisible et devenir, en pratique, une forme de domestication. Ceci est souvent considéré comme de la préservation plus que de la conservation. Parallèlement, la conservation in situ, au moins en théorie, permet aux populations végétales de se développer et d’évoluer dans, ou en faisant partie de, l’écosystème de leur habitat naturel. En pratique, les deux méthodes devraient être considérées comme des approches complémentaires et se renforçant mutuellement.

La conservation ex-situ dans les jardins botaniques a plusieurs avantages et peut être la seule option disponible lorsque l’habitat naturel a été détruit.

Il existe trois jardins botaniques institutionnels à Dakar: deux à l'Université; le troisième dépend du MEA. Tous trois sont soucieux de conservation des espèces végétales. Un autre jardin a été installé dans un grand parc par l’ONG ENDA-Tiers Monde à Mbour. Ils ont des approches différentes et complémentaires.

overview_statement:
Chaboco Natura – Jardín Botánico Lanzarote is a developing botanic garden located in Lanzarote (Canary Islands, Spain), focused on the conservation, research, and education of native and endemic flora from arid volcanic island ecosystems. The garden combines documented living collections with an emerging seed bank (germplasm collection) to support the ex situ conservation of priority species characteristic of coastal, halophytic, psammophilous, and xerophytic habitats.

Established as part of the activities of the environmental association Arrecife Natura, the project integrates conservation action with environmental education and applied research. Living collections are structured to represent key plant communities of Lanzarote and La Graciosa, while seed collections are developed following established protocols for long-term conservation, including controlled drying, viability monitoring, and storage at −18 °C.

Chaboco Natura contributes to plant conservation through seed collection, propagation, on-site habitat management, and the implementation of small-scale restoration actions in degraded urban and peri-urban environments. The garden also delivers educational programmes, technical training, and field-based learning activities aimed at connecting local communities with native biodiversity and conservation practice.

Current priorities include the expansion and documentation of collections, the consolidation of seed bank operations in line with international standards, and the development of collaborations with regional and international institutions to support research, capacity building, and the long-term conservation of Canary Islands flora.
mission_statement: Chaboco Natura – Jardín Botánico Lanzarote is a living centre dedicated to the conservation of native and endemic flora of the Canary Islands, rooted in the arid volcanic landscape of Lanzarote. Through documented living collections, seed banking, research, and education, it connects people with the unique plant diversity of these islands and the ecological processes that sustain them. The garden cultivates knowledge, restoration, and the long-term conservation of plant life in fragile dryland ecosystems.

overview_statement:
The “Jardí botànic de la Universitat de València” is one of the oldest botanical gardens in Spain. It was founded in 1567, and for a long time it was the only one. It was originally thought as a garden for the teaching of medicinal herbs in the 16th century. Nowadays, the JBUV’s mission is to become a centre of excellence in research, conservation, education and understanding. Its aim is to contribute to a better management of the Earth’s environment by increasing knowledge, awareness and understanding of the Plant Kingdom, which is the basis of life on Earth, its importance and its conservation.


The JBUV is one of the most valued heritage landmarks of the city of Valencia. Recently it has been declared a place of cultural and historical interest. In its research building (inaugurated in 2000) scientific, cultural and educational activities take place. We can also find the University of Valencia herbarium (with more than 200,000 specimens), a specialized library and a seed bank of Valencian and Mediterranean threatened flora.

All this near a beautiful garden of centenary trees with more than 4,500 cultivated species.

overview_statement:
The second largest botanical garden in Sri Lanka, Hakgala Botanical Gardens is picturesquely situated in the hill country, a mere ten kilometres (six miles) away from the city of Nuwara Eliya. The comfortable cool weather that prevails throughout the year compliments the exotic flora and fauna, creating a true paradise.

According to the legends, the history of Hakgala Gardens dates back to the time of Ramayanaya; an epic love story of the east. Queen Sita, captured and brought to Sri Lanka, is said to have been hidden in this vicinity - the Hakgala Gardens at that time was one of the pleasure gardens of King Ravana.

The present day Hakgala Gardens was established in 1861 under the patronage of Dr G H W Thawaites. Originally it was used for the cultivation of cinchona and later for tea. The development of Hakgala Gardens as a botanic garden was initiated by Mr William Nock and since then many varieties of flowers and trees, both local and foreign, have been introduced.

A network of small creeks, complete with wooden bridges, is seen throughout the garden, creating a magical atmosphere. The magnificent rose garden, conifers, cedars, cypresses, variety of pines and English oak are just a few examples of the diversity of plant life that is seen here.

overview_statement:
Konya Tropical Butterfly Garden

 

In our garden, 20.000 plants belonging to 195 distinct species accompany our visitors during the trip. There are many plants in Turkey that visitors can only see in our garden. Plants were selected from those with the most suitable sepal structure for the butterfly's feeding. No pesticides are used in our garden in order not to harm the living life. To improve the quality of life in the garden, plants that can absorb harmful substances in the environment and have high oxygen production are preferred.

In the construction of Konya Tropical Butterfly Garden and Insect Museum, 630 tons of steel and 1,730 glass coating systems, each in varied sizes, were used. In addition, a special PVB material was used, which allows the maximum passage of UV rays, which facilitates the butterflies to find their way.

The building has the distinction of being the first LEED Certified Museum in Turkey. In its construction, energy efficient equipment, sunshades, efficient glasses were used, and it was designed with high energy efficiency. The water efficiency of the building is 47% and the energy efficiency is 12%. Interior material quality is at the highest level.

It has a large internal volume that can sustain extremely sensitive living species and has VOC paint, coating and insulation materials that do not contain volatile/semi-volatile organic chemical compounds. An enormous infrastructure system works under the building to create the natural environment of the butterflies. Thanks to this system, the tropical garden part is kept at 80% humidity and a temperature of 26±20C. Konya Tropical Butterfly Garden is a vivarium that you will hardly find in the world.

In Konya Tropical Garden, on an area of ​​2200 m², there are a pedestrian path that progresses at different levels, shaped with artificial rocks and ponds, landscaped with special plants, where butterflies can be observed in their natural habitat; tropical butterfly garden and sections where pupa formations can be seen, 400 m² insect museum with visual objects related to different insect species; 90 m² movie theater where there will be projection presentations about life cycles; 200 m² multi-purpose hall and 200 m² cafeteria facilities.

In the museum section, it is possible to see the larval stage of butterflies from their eggs to an adult butterfly. In the Butterfly Behavior section, 11 different behaviors of butterflies in nature can be seen. These are courtship, fruit feeding, sunbathing, protection, active pseudo-eye, passive pseudo-eye, mud bath, mating, nectar feeding, egg laying, camouflage behaviors. Trips to the world of insects are made with short films shown in the insect cinema. In the Butterfly Classification section, the magnificent colors of butterflies belonging to 6 different butterfly families can be examined. In the Insect Museum section, it can be seen that the eggs belonging to the Hymenoptera, Mantodea, Coleoptera, Odonata and Phasmatodea orders are magnified 50 thousand times and how the insects in these eggs actually take place in our lives. In addition, rhinoceros beetles, queen bees, leaf beetles and stick beetles that normally cannot be seen in our country are exhibited. Perhaps, the concept of right and wrong with insects can be questioned again.

Konya Tropical Butterfly Garden, which was built in the form of a butterfly in accordance with nature, was established to instill a love of nature and animals to our children. We aim to leave a different memory to our visitors' lives by enabling them to see animals and plants that they cannot encounter in their daily lives.

Among the aims of our garden are to enable adults, especially children, to get to know nature and some species of living things, to encourage positive feelings towards nature, to eliminate prejudices against these creatures, and to create a bond with living things in nature.

In the education classrooms of our garden, our student visitors from schools can participate in mini programs in the field they choose, where they can provide detailed information and close contact. Our insect, interesting creatures and reptile education are tailored to the education levels of our students. First of all, information is given depending on the subject of the chosen field, and it is aimed to give fun and remarkable information to our students rather than giving an education based on rote learning. Afterwards, it is aimed to reinforce the knowledge and overcome the fears that may exist against the living thing by ensuring that they come into contact with the living things that they theoretically know by receiving training. At the end of the training program, various activities related to the subject are conducted with the students according to the age group.

Apart from the education classes, we also have some activities for high school and college students and adult visitors. With the activities we have prepared in the cinema section, we aim to change their perspectives towards nature by learning facts about animals that they know very differently. In the event we call "Touch the Life", visitors witness the first flapping of wings of butterflies and admire one of the most beautiful miracle of creation.

 

Konya Tropical Butterfly Garden Nature Education Class

It is a quite important and vital issue for humanity to be aware of its responsibilities towards nature and to know which path to follow to protect it, in order for the ecosystem existing on Earth to continue in a healthy manner. As Konya Tropical Butterfly Garden, we believe that the most effective and definitive method of creating this awareness is conscious nature education given at an early age. For this reason, with our nature education programs that we have prepared for every age group and education level, we do not only provide our students with information about the living life and environment, support their active learning by experiencing this information one by one, but also aim to remind that we are also a part of this nature.

 

Topics in our Nature Education program

1)   Explore the Colorful World of Insects

Insects are a very crowded and colorful group of creatures that cover almost 70% of the animals on earth. It is of vital importance to recognize insects, which are at the basis of the world's ecosystem together with plants, and to learn and apply the methods of protecting them. Although both the ecological and economic relations between insects and humans are quite strong, we misunderstand them and pass on our needless fears from generation to generation. In our education class, we explain why this living group is important and should be protected, in the simplest way, and enable them to contact them. Our training, which lasts about 45 minutes, includes a presentation in which short information is shared, contact with living things, training activities and distribution of certificates approved by our institution that they have completed the training. Afterwards, they complete the education process by visiting the tropical garden area, which is rich in plant and butterfly species, accompanied by expert biologist guides.

2)   Let's Meet Reptiles

Reptiles are one of the groups that are feared as well as attracting attention among living groups. Their quiet and relatively secret lives have always attracted the attention of mankind. In addition, reptiles are among the most important living groups that ensure the balance in the ecosystem. Getting to know nature and its creatures will both make our lives easier and prevent the fears that wear us out. With our reptilian education, it is aimed that our students get to know this mysterious living group and learn how to contact them correctly and in a controlled manner without harming them and living things. Our training, which lasts about 45 minutes, includes a presentation in which short information is shared, contact with the live, training activities and distribution of certificates approved by our institution that they have completed the training. Afterwards, they complete the education process by visiting the tropical garden area, which is rich in plant and butterfly species, accompanied by expert biologist guides.

3)   I'm Among Interesting Creatures

Nature has always been the habitat and source of life for humanity. However, environmental pollution and global warming, the effects of which we have felt so much lately, clearly show that the harmony that exists between us and nature has deteriorated. One of the most important reasons for this is that we, as humanity, have lost our curiosity and interest in nature. For this reason, there are situations where we harm nature voluntarily or unintentionally. Our goal is to strengthen our ties with nature at an early age, thanks to this education. For this reason, in the education of interesting creatures, we aim to both recognize the living thing and reinforce the instinct to protect nature by explaining the physical or behavioral characteristics of some living things in nature, which make their life easier and attract our attention because we have never seen or heard of them. . Our training, which lasts about 45 minutes, includes a presentation in which short information is shared, contact with the live, training activities and distribution of certificates approved by our institution that they have completed the training. Afterwards, they complete the education process by visiting the tropical garden area, which is rich in plant and butterfly species, accompanied by expert biologist guides.

Some of the projects we have completed as Konya Tropical Butterfly Garden

1)   School Garden and Insect House

As in the other countries of the world, the applications in which the student continues the education process by spending active time with nature also attract a lot of attention in our country. This project, under the name of 'School Garden and Insect House', was carried out by the Selçuklu Municipality/Konya Tropical Butterfly Garden in four public schools at the kindergarten and primary level in the Konya/Selçuklu region between 24-27 May 2022. The aim of the project is for the student to experience the productivity of nature, to touch the soil, to work for production and to see the greenery of his labor. The aim of the project is to adopt the idea of 'Permaculture-Based School Gardens', which is indispensable for an education process in harmony with nature. In this project concept, which consists of three main elements; It consists of vegetable beds where vegetable seedlings will grow, a compost area that will create efficient fertilizer for vegetable beds, as well as a compost area that will support recycling, and an insect house that will enable the observation of the insect fauna of the region, which has an indispensable place in the ecosystem cycle, as well as plant development. Within the scope of the project, the seedlings were planted together with our students and teachers in the schools involved in the project, under suitable weather conditions, and necessary information was given. The preparatory phase of the project, its implementation and its positive contribution to the anticipated training process were realized as intended.

2)   Wandering Nature-Long Live the Butterfly-My Village School

As Selçuklu Municipality Konya Tropical Butterfly Garden, the main purpose of our project called 'My Village Schools', which is the first step of the 'Wandering Nature - Long Live the Butterfly!' project; To introduce the Konya Tropical Butterfly Garden by reaching our children in some educational institutions that are economically and transportation disadvantaged, and to help them overcome their fear of living creatures while increasing their knowledge about butterflies, which are indispensable for the ecosystem.

3)   Wandering Nature-Long Live the Butterfly - Konya Seljuk State Kindergartens

As Selçuklu Municipality Konya Tropical Butterfly Garden, 'Wandering Nature – Long Live Butterfly! - The main purpose of the project named 'Konya Selçuklu State Kindergartens' is to transform the kindergarten period, which is the most productive and permanent education age of children, into an environment where active nature education is given. With the schools designated as the Konya Tropical Butterfly Garden, training was given on the life cycle of butterflies, their benefits and methods of preventing environmental pollution, and the level of knowledge about living things was increased by nurturing children's curiosity.

4)   Konya Tropical Butterfly Garden Nature Science Festival

Our festival, where we brought nature and science together, both provided information-filled moments and entertained the participants.

5)   Workshops

While you are wandering around our tropical garden with pleasure, you can come across our activity workshops from a corner at any time. There is brief information about various creatures and fun activities.

6)   Touch to Life

In our event called Touch to Life, our butterflies, which come from pupa to adult winged form, make their first flight from the hands of our visitors.

7)   Movie Event

In the activities we have prepared for student groups in the cinema section, we aim to change their perspectives towards nature by learning facts about animals that they know very differently.

 

Tropical Garden Area

It is the largest butterfly garden in Europe with its 2000m² tropical area. Every year, more than 150,000 butterflies of 75 different species from countries in the tropical climate zones such as the Philippines, Kenya, Costa Rica, and Panama come to the Konya Tropical Butterfly Garden in the pupa stage. These incoming pupae pass into the adult stage, which is the last stage of their lives, and become butterflies. Our facility, which has hosted 2,513,019 visitors since its opening, aims to raise awareness of nature and increase interest in nature by introducing tropical butterflies to visitors. Our expert biologist team working in the garden contributes to the development of nature awareness in the most effective way by conveying scientific information about living things to visitors of all ages in an entertaining way.

 

Insect Museum Section

In the Life Cycle area, which is the first part of the Konya Tropical Butterfly Garden Insect Museum, the formation stages of the butterfly (egg, caterpillar, pupa, and adult butterfly) are exhibited. In the Insect Cinema, by broadcasting entertaining movies about insects, allows guests to have a pleasant break. In the Butterfly Classification section, which includes six families of butterflies, tablets containing information about the families and different types of real dried butterflies belonging to these families are exhibited. The section of Butterfly Behavior, you can watch what butterflies do in nature, how they live, and how they are protected from their predators in their struggle for survival. The last part of the museum is the Insect Village, where there are huge insect eggs made with 50,000 times magnification. Apart from butterflies, there are real dried samples of insects belonging to five different orders, as well as information such as how human beings benefited from these insects and what was invented by looking at insects.

·         Hymenoptera

·         Mantodea

·         Coleoptera

·         Odonata

·         Phasmatodea

 

Butterfly Collection

The second most populous order of the insect class is the lepidoptera. They have been the order that attracted the most attention of photographers and collectors. Various dried butterflies from all over the world are included in our collection.

overview_statement: Winterbourne Botanic Garden at the University of Birmingham is a six acre Edwardian Arts and Crafts style garden on the university's Edgbaston Campus. The garden is a haven of peace and tranquillity only 15 minutes from the city centre. We hold three National Collections and have lots of interesting features to see including colour themed borders, a pergola, Japanese bridge and unusual sandstone rock garden. This was originally a private garden (1903) and was bequeathed to the university in 1944. The Garden retains many original features and planting, including a 100 year old, 32m long, nut walk of Corylus avellana. The National Collections include: - the History of the European Rose, - Anthemis spp. - Iris unguicularis spp.

overview_statement:
The NIE was established in December 2013 to lead the ecological research in Korea and globally to strengthen national competitiveness and contribute to environmental conservation and foster proper environmental awareness by providing citizens with various opportunities to experience and learn about ecosystems. It consists of the main institute, the Endangered Species Restoration Center, and the Wetland Center located in Seocheon, Chungcheongnam-do, Yeongyang, Gyeongsangbuk-do, Changnyeong-gun, Gyeongsangnam-do, respectively.

As an agency under the Ministry of Environment, which serves as the Management Authority for Convention on International Trade in Endangered Species of Wild Fauna and Flora (CITES), the National Institute of Ecology supports the proper implementation of the convention in Korea. Since 2017, it has been designated as a biological resource conservation facility, fulfilling the role of a national platform for securing, conserving, researching, utilizing, and educating about biological resources, including plants. Additionally, it is designated as a CITES Shelter, an international facility for the protection of endangered animals.

As an ecological research institution, the National Institute of Ecology supports national policies by conducting statutory commissioned research projects, such as the National Natural Environment Survey and the management of invasive alien species. By conducting diverse ecological research serving as the foundation for environmental conservation, it has established itself as a leading ecological research institution. The Endangered Species Restoration Center of the institute is the first specialized institution for endangered species research and restoration of the nation, conducting artificial propagation and restoration, biological specimen banking and habitat management, reintroduction programs, and regular training for ex-situ conservation institutions. Finally, the Wetland Center conducts surveys and research activities for the efficient conservation and management of wetland ecosystems.

Simultaneously, in the outdoor exhibition area of the main institute, wetlands restored based on Ramsar-listed wetlands, the Korean Peninsula Forest modeled after Korean mountainous forests, and landscapes of the DMZ that showcase the power of regeneration of nature are present. In the indoor exhibition area, the Ecorium exists, a greenhouse and comprehensive space for ecological research, exhibition, and education where visitors can observe and experience the ecosystems of the five major climate zones. The Ecorium offers various special exhibitions, events, and experiential ecological education programs each year. Additionally, through various types of publications utilizing the results of research, education, and exhibition projects, the institute strives to convey accurate ecological knowledge and information.
mission_statement: The National Institute of Ecology (NIE) targets the realizing of a sustainable future through the conservation of the ecosystem and dissemination of ecological values. By continuously promoting research, exhibitions, and educational activities for ecological enhancement, it aims to become a national ecological platform for the coexistence of nature and humans.

overview_statement:
Paignton Zoo is part of Wild Planet Trust, formerly Whitley Wildlife Conservation Trust, is a registered education, scientific and conservation charity established in 1957 and based in Devon, UK.

We own two zoos in southwest England, two local nature reserves and a National Nature Reserve. We are active in conservation at home and abroad, often working alongside partner organisations to conserve species and their habitats.

Located in Devon, Paignton Zoo is one of the South West’s most exciting visitor attractions. It’s a place to roam, discover, explore and get in touch with nature. With over 2,000 animals and countless amazing plants (TAXA 2,990 (1,600 spp., 5.138 accessions, 20,000 plants) across 80 acres of beautiful, spacious grounds and tropical and arid houses.
mission_statement:
Here at Wild Planet Trust, we have a very important mission.

We act to protect at-risk animals and plants from the impacts of biodiversity loss in order to Help Halt Species Decline

We focus on helping humans understand how to live in harmony with nature

We believe that…

Every species is important

Everything is connected

Every action matters

We bring our mission to life through our START programme, which shapes who we are and what we do:

S = Safe havens

We identify, improve and create safe havens for threatened species both here in the UK and abroad.

T = Togetherness

We work together with community and project partnerships to create deep, long-lasting change.

A = Action

We take action to protect and establish sustainable habitats, such as protecting seagrass meadows in Torbay, and promoting the use of sustainable palm oil in food and household products.

R = Research

We conduct research to advance animal welfare and conservation science.

T = Talk

We talk to people about the vital nature of our work and show them how they can make real, achievable change in their own lives and communities.

overview_statement: The Agnes Scott Arboretum is an extension and reflection of the liberal arts curriculum of Agnes Scott College, a historic college for women in Atlanta, Georgia. Since 1889, Agnes Scott College has educated women to think deeply, live honorably, and engage the intellectual and social challenges of their times. Its 100-acre campus is home to more than 2000 trees, which contribute greatly to its reputation as one of the most beautiful colleges in the country. Some of its notable trees were donated by alumnae and planted by members of the faculty, staff, and student body.

Established in 2000, the Allegheny Arboretum encompasses the entire 374 acres of the Indiana University of Pennsylvania campus, including a 150-acre woodland. In 2005, the Allegheny Arboretum officially became part of the university and is overseen by the Allegheny Arboretum Board, which provides guidance in meeting the arboretum’s goals and objectives.
