overview_statement: The Acton Arboretum is situated on 65 acres of town conservation land in the heart of Town Center, Acton, Massachusetts. The Arboretum boasts a trail system through open meadows, beside woodland ponds, along a glacial esker, and through a bog. A handicapped accessible trail provides access to the herb garden, butterfly garden, hosta garden, daylily garden, rhododendron garden, lilac fragrance garden, and a pond wetland. The Wildflower Trail provides access to a wide range of woodland habitats. Parking is available at the Arboretum’s main entrance, off Taylor Road. Much of the area adjacent to the parking lot is handicapped-accessible, and is open, with stone-dust or paved paths, gardens, bridges, and picnic tables. Trails and paths crisscross the entire area.

The Arboretum at Starin Park (AASP) will—long into the future—be providing a beautiful, welcoming sanctuary for humans, native trees, shrubs, and perennials, and for wildlife. It will be a place where people of all ages can come to connect to nature, learn about the environment, and study and practice stewardship.  The Arboretum at Starin Park is be dedicated to helping create a greener, healthier, and more beautiful world.

Over time, AASP will create and maintain a living collection (a kind of museum) of native Wisconsin plants. It also intends to become a regional hub of the Homegrown National Park movement. Working with the University of Wisconsin, Whitewater, AASP will provide biodiversity workshops and training and other resources to the communities of southeast Wisconsin.

The Arboretum At Starin Park will be a cooperative partnership between the City of Whitewater, Whitewater Unified School District, The University of Wisconsin, Whitewater, the Historic Starin Park Neighborhood Association, and corporate sponsors yet to be determined.

Overview

Managed by Trees Atlanta, in partnership with Atlanta Beltline, Inc., Atlanta Beltline Partnership, and the City of Atlanta Department of Parks and Recreation, the Atlanta Beltline Arboretum is a public garden centered on promoting native plants through education, restoration, demonstration, and display.

overview_statement:
Around 1930, the Arboretum Heverleebos at Oud-Heverlee researched how non-native trees respond to the prevailing climate.

From 2000, it was decided to make the collection more varied. Open spaces, rest areas and footpaths were created.

The domain is 9 hectares in size and contains about 300 different species, native and non-native.

The arboretum includes an American maple tree, ginkgo, golden larch, Japanese biscuit tree, juniper and a wild apple. The tall giant sequoias were planted in 1961.

In het Arboretum Heverleebos in Oud-Heverlee wordt rond 1930 onderzocht hoe uitheemse bomen reageren op het hier heersende klimaat.

Vanaf 2000 wordt er beslist om de verzameling gevarieerder te maken. Er zijn open plekken, rustzones en wandelpaden aangelegd.

Het domein is 9 ha groot en bevat ongeveer 300 verschillende soorten, inheems en exotisch.

In het arboretum staan onder meer een Amerikaanse slangenesdoorn, ginkgo, goudlork, Japanse koekjesboom, jeneverbes en wilde appel. De hoge mammoetbomen zijn in 1961 aangeplant.

overview_statement:
Arboretum Groenendaal is the oldest arboretum in Belgium. It was set up in 1897 by order of King Leopold II to investigate which non-native tree species are useful for Belgian forestry. Now it has no longer that function, the arboretum is managed ecologically.

The arboretum is 14 hectares in size. The design is simple but takes advantage of the natural relief.  The collection consists 120 different conifers and 330 deciduous trees. 90% of the collection consists of non-native species.  There are some impressive old and large trees in Groenendaal, such as the 40 meters high common sequoia (Sequoiadendron giganteum), with a circumference of 4,80 meters, the coastal redwood (Sequoia sempervirens) and the Hickery nut (Carya cordiformis).

Arboretum Groenendaal is het oudste arboretum van België. Het wordt in 1897 in opdracht van Koning Leopold II opgezet om te onderzoeken welke uitheemse boomsoorten bruikbaar zijn voor de Belgische bosbouw. Die functie heeft het nu niet meer, het arboretum wordt nu ecologisch beheerd.

Het arboretum is 14 ha groot. Het ontwerp is eenvoudig maar maakt gebruik van het natuurlijke reliëf.  De collectie bestaat uit 120 verschillende coniferen en 330 loofbomen. 90% van de collectie bestaat uit uitheemse soorten.  Er staan in Groenendaal enkele indrukwekkende oude en grote bomen, zoals de veertig meter hoge, gewone mammoetboom (Sequoiadendron giganteum), met een omtrek van 4,80 meter, de kustmammoetboom (Sequoia sempervirens)  en de Hickerynoot (Carya cordiformis).

overview_statement:
The former agricultural detention college situated in the beautiful surroundings of the Merksplas Colony is now a remarkable showcase of horticultural gems.There are several exceptional collections to be admired here including Hydrangea, Agapanthus, Paeonia, Hamamelis, Hemeroacallis and many more besides.

 

The garden is the lifework of plant breeder Jan Oprins and the botanical testament of the late Harry Van Trier, renowned botanist.The site has subsequently expanded to accommodate the collections of many plant enthousiasts. One such person, Jan Hendrickx,has since 2015 devoted himself to the implementation and design of this peaceful haven.

 

In 2020 the botanical garden “De Kleine Boerderij” Merksplas npo became a member of The Association of Botanical Gardens and Arboreta (V.B.T.A vzw).

 

This impressive garden is fundamentally a functional space, focussing on nature, education and wellbeing. As a source of inspiration, a place to meet or a tranquil place to relax. All are welcome.

 

At the heart of this enterprise is an enthusiastic group of volunteers, who are assisted by youth and adults who work as part of the care farm work. Every day lend their services to the upkeep and running of the garden and adjacent café. Allowing you to enjoy a leisurely walk followed by a light refreshment. A perfect day out!
mission_statement: At collection garden 'De Kleine Boerderij Merksplas', we are committed to cultivating a vibrant and inclusive botanical sanctuary where nature, education, and community come together. Our mission is to preserve and expand exceptional plant collections while fostering a deep appreciation for horticulture and biodiversity. Through dedicated care, sustainable practices, and the involvement of passionate volunteers, we create a space that inspires, heals, and connects people of all backgrounds. We strive to be a place of tranquility, learning, and social engagement—where every visitor can find beauty, knowledge, and a sense of belonging.

overview_statement:
With more than 15 000 species and varieties of plants cultivated on more than 70 hectares, the Jardin Botanique de Paris carries out its missions of conservation and study flora diversity, engage in dialogue with the scientific community, improve the public’s understanding of the collections, with four sites from the East and the West of the capital: 
the Jardin des Serres d’Auteuil and its tropical landscapes,
the Parc de Bagatelle and its internationally renowned rose gardens,
the Parc Floral de Paris and its regional flora,
the Arboretum de Paris and its trees from temperate regions all over the world.

Founded in 1995, the Jardin Botanique de Paris has been recognized by the Association des jardins botaniques de France et des pays francophones (The association of botanic gardens of France and french-speaking countries) since 1998. The Jardin Botanique de Paris has a bank seed of regional flora and publishes an Index Seminum.   

Many events take place in the Parc Floral de Paris and the Parc de Bagatelle: concerts, photo exhibitions,… Every year, in these parks and in the Jardin des Serres d’Auteuil and the Arboretum, a botanic exhibition take place : in 2018 the topic will be « Plants and insects ».

overview_statement:
St. Petersburg Botanical Garden is one of the oldest in our country. The Garden served as the basis for an "Apothecary garden", founded by Peter I in 1714 for the cultivation of medicinal herbs, as well as rare and interesting foreign plants. The growth of the collections and the importance of the botanical studies led to the establishment in 1823 of the Imperial Botanical Garden. During the years 1823-1824 is built quads greenhouses, which largely survive to this day. At the same time, the grounds were created. By 1913, the Garden became the national center of plant science and one of the leading botanical institutions in the world.

Two articles written on the collections of the Komarov Botanical Institute's Botanical Garden:

Tkachenko K. G., Pautova I. A., Korobova M. M. The Introduction Nursery of Food, Crop and Medicinal Plants at the Komarov Botanical Institute of the Russian Academy of Sciences: its role in the conservation of biodiversity // Botanic Gardens Conservation News. 1997. Vol. 2, N 8. P. 38-40.

Smirnov Y.S., Tkachenko K.G. The Botanical Garden of the Komarov Botanical Institute of the Russian Academy of Science celebrate 285 years // Botanical Collections and Biodiversity. Linnean Society occasional Publications 3, 2001. London, Westbury Publishing. P. 109-115.

overview_statement:
Central Siberian Botanical Garden of the Siberian Branch of the Russian Academy of Sciences is the largest botanical institution in the Asian part of Russia. It was founded in the West Siberian Division of the USSR Academy of Sciences on academician V. L. Komarov's initiative in 1946.
Central Siberian Botanical Garden is a center of integration of botanical and ecological research in Siberia. Council of Siberian Botanical Gardens, Council for Problems of Botany in Siberia, Council for Protected Objects of the Plant Life and Novosibirsk Branch of the Russian Botanical Society work at the institution.
CSBG, SB RAS is a member of Botanic Gardens Conservation International. The scientists take part in different joint projects with the USA, Italy, Finland, Canada, Sweden, China and other countries.

Training of highly qualified personnel for research institutions and educational establishments of Siberia through graduate and post-graduate studies is an importantpart of the work of CSBG. There is a Dissertation Committee on Ecology and Botany.

More than 70 patents on the inventions and cultivars of food, medicinal and ornamental plants have been obtained by the specialists of CSBG.

A number of collections and experimental plots have been created to date and new ones are being created within the Garden. These include an arboretum consisting of 400 species, 166 forms and hybrids, a medicinal, spicy and aromatic plant garden (350 species), collections of forage plants (270 species), rare and endangered plants (more than 100 species), ornamental plants (428 species) and food plants (144 species). There is also an extensive tropical collection held in the glasshouses consisting of 3000 species of tropical and subtropical plants. Experimental plots "Stony garden", "Garden of continuous flowering" and "Bonsai"are significant for this region. There are two herbaria with 550,000 specimens, a seed collection (1220 species) and a big collection of lichens and fungi.
Much of the basic and applied work that CSBG undertakes is in the form of the publication of 170 monographs, numerous collections and articles. In recent years publications have included a 14-volume "Flora of Siberia", "Green Data Book of Siberia", "Red Data Books" of certain regions of Siberia and "Manuals for the Identification of Plants"of Novosibrsk and Kemerovo Oblasts. "Siberian Journal of Ecology" is published.

overview_statement: The mission of The John Bartram Arboretum at Kendal at Oberlin is to be a model of responsible urban arboriculture to engage, sustain, and educate our residents and the broader community.

The Arboretum at the Ringling consist of over 2,300 trees that represent both native and exotic species.  The arboretum, which covers 66 acres, boasts an impressive collection of trees, among them 14 Banyan (Ficus altissima), the largest collection in Florida; Shaving Brush (pseudobombax ellipticum); Coral Tree (Erythrina variegate); Bunya Bunya Tree (Araucaria bidwilli); Rainbow Eucalyptus (Eucalyptus deglupta); and over 30 species of palms. Included in the lush collection is Florida's Millennium Landmark Tree, a Banyan, located near the Ca'd'Zan driveway. The Millennium Tree Trail at the southern end of the estate, created as part of the National Millennium Arbor Day Celebration, provides a welcome respite from the intense Florida sun and showcases a wide variety of trees, including oak, holly, citrus, and magnolia.

organisation_name: The University of Texas at Austin
overview_statement: The campus landscape of The University of Texas at Austin serves as an unconventional arboretum dedicated to a diverse collection of both native and adapted tree species for Central Texas. It is a community forest providing shaded escape into green spaces, opportunities for education and research, and habitat for pollinators and wildlife. The university hosts annual events to engage students, faculty and staff in the celebration and care of campus trees. Almost 5,000 trees are inventoried, with information, assessed values and ecosystem benefits available for public access online.

The THP (about 10 ha) is nicknamed “Noah’s Ark”, reminiscing the biblical event, when lives were saved from a ravaging flood! This status is based on merit as the THP hosts ex-situ collections of over 100 species of native trees, about half of which are classified as threatened and/or endemic. Located within the campus of the International Institute of Tropical Agriculture (IITA) in Ibadan, Nigeria, the park was started in the early 1990s as an agroforestry arboretum incorporating both food and forest crops, which were either native or non-native. In 2015, it was restored for the conservation of rare and endangered Nigerian trees–thanks to the donors that provided funding. In addition to serving as a repository of genetic resources, the THP provides opportunities for promoting environmental education. Thus, the park hosts facilities for visiting tourists, schoolchildren and family groups, including adventure playground, forest classroom, hide and boardwalk, barbecue pavilion, natural history museum and campsite.

Washington University was founded in St. Louis in 1853 as the city underwent an historic period of growth. The university’s hilltop campus known today as the Danforth Campus, was established in 1900, and consists of 169 acres featuring a diverse collection of trees. Today the 7,000 plus trees on campus range from well-established historical trees to newly planted, climate resilient ones. Currently there are 400 plus species of native and adaptive trees on campus. The Arboretum of Washington University serves Danforth Campus and the St. Louis region as a living laboratory for everyone to enjoy by promoting environmental appreciation and sustainability on campus. With each tree planted in the arboretum, Washington University becomes more integrated with its surrounding landscape, blending with the beautiful tree-lined neighborhood streets and nearby Forest Park.
mission_statement:
The mission of Washington University in St. Louis is to act in service of truth through the formation of leaders, the discovery of knowledge and the treatment of patients for the betterment of our region, our nation and our world.

At WashU, we generate, disseminate, and apply knowledge. We foster freedom of inquiry and expression of ideas in our research, teaching and learning.

We aim to create an environment that encourages and supports wide-ranging exploration at the frontier of discovery by embracing diverse perspectives from individuals of all identities and backgrounds. We promote higher education and rigorous research as a fundamental component of an open, vibrant society. We strive to enhance the lives and livelihoods not only of our students, patients, and employees but also of the people of the greater St. Louis community and beyond. We do so by addressing scientific, social, economic, medical, and other challenges in the local, national, and international realms.

OUR GOALS ARE:

  • to foster excellence and creativity in our teaching, research, scholarship, patient care and service

  • to welcome students, faculty and staff from all backgrounds to create an inclusive, equitable community that is nurturing and intellectually rigorous

  • to cultivate in students habits of lifelong learning and critical and ethical thinking, thereby enabling them to be productive members and leaders of a global society

  • to contribute positively to our home community of St. Louis, and to effect meaningful, constructive change in our world

TO THIS END WE INTEND:

  • to hold ourselves to the highest standards of excellence

  • to educate aspiring leaders of great ability from diverse backgrounds

  • to encourage faculty and students to be innovative, bold, independent, critical thinkers

  • to build an inclusive, equitable, respectful, ethically-principled environment for living, teaching, learning and working for the present and future generations

  • to focus on meaningful and measurable outcomes for all of our endeavors

The tree collection at UCC has joined some of the leading arboreta in the world after being accredited internationally by Arbnet in 2020. Some of the highlights of the collection include a pair of c. 150 year old Giant Redwoods (Sequoia sempervirens giganteum); the Strawberry Tree (Arbutos unedo), an Irish native; an Irish champion Wing Nut (Pterocarya fraxinifolia); and collection of mature pines (including Scots, Monteray and Bhutan pines). organisation_name_alt: Quinta de los Molinos Garden, Habana
overview_statement:
The Botanic Garden of Havana "Quinta de los Molinos” is considered the flagship environmental center of the Office of the Historian of the City of Havana. In the same physical space and over a little more than two centuries, several events come together and intertwine to give rise to an interesting story.

This space owes its name to the existence of a tobacco mill called San Francisco de Asís, belonging to the Royal Tobacco Factory of Havana in the final years of the 18th century. These tobacco mills of the Royal Factory were moved by the water of the Zanja Real (the first hydraulic work in Havana and Cuba) and turned the aromatic and fragrant leaf into snuff powder. As the years went by and the City grew and became what it is today, this place was located on the central Avenida Salvador Allende (formerly called Carlos III), between G and Calzada de Infanta streets.

In this site of great history where nature and heritage harmonize, the great diversity of its flora stands out with very old species, originating from the first botanical garden in Havana and Cuba. It was founded on May 30, 1817, in an area of ​​Havana known, during the Spanish Colony, as Campo de Marte. Today, this area corresponds to the south wing of the National Capitol and the Parque de la Fraternidad. In 1839, due to the construction of the first railway station here, the Botanic Garden was moved to the land adjacent to the rest house of the Captains General, remaining there until 1968. Like most botanical gardens, this one was transferred to the University in 1872, then the site was considered an important reference in the World System of Botanic Gardens.

It is worth noting that due to its natural and built values, the Quinta de los Molinos was declared a National Monument in 1981 by the National Commission of Monuments, as it is considered one of the emblematic places of the city, of great historical importance due to its close links to the emergence of Cuba as a nation.

In the 1990s, the Quinta de los Molinos experienced a period of decline, abandonment and deterioration of its facilities and gardens. In 2005, the administration of the institution was transferred from the Ministry of Culture to the Office of the City Historian, and from 2006 to the present, a major restoration process began on the 5 hectares. The intense investment process (historians, archaeologists, architects, engineers, builders, investors, botanists, etc.) together with researchers from the Institute of Ecology and Systematics, the Ministry of Science, Technology and Environment (CITMA) among other institutions, was divided into several stages and different objects of work. The criterion for intervening in all the areas was to completely rehabilitate it, maintaining the existing spaces and rescuing the architectural and natural values ​​of its different construction phases. Recovering each compositional element was quite a challenge.

The workers had to make a huge effort to turn this place into a beautiful green lung in the center of the city of Havana. The restored areas were regaining their splendor, so that the Quinta became a very unique place, where nature, heritage, history and aesthetics were intertwined.

Botanic Garden of Havana "Quinta de los Molinos” – innovative and inclusive

In October 2022, an SME was approved for the administration of the Botanic Garden of Havana "Quinta de los Molinos”. This public medium-sized company has a sole partner, the Office of the Historian of the City of Havana. "La Quinta" Company operates as a social contribution company, allocating all its income to social and environmental projects.

This company manages the 4.7 hectare forest space, which houses a wealth of 350 species of plants, and more than 20 endemic species of Cuba. Many of the tree species that survive today were bred from the previous location of the botanical garden, so they have heritage value, having been planted on this site since 1935. The trees also provide a refuge for fauna: insects, reptiles, mollusks and others.

In close collaboration with the Faculty of Biology of the University of Havana, it has been determined that this botanical garden is a resting area during bird migrations, housing a wealth of 270 bird species, being considered an important site for bird conservation in Havana.

La Quinta S.U.R.L. is considered an inclusive company: today we employs more than 20 people with intellectual disabilities through a labor inclusion programme. In addition, about 50 young people with disabilities benefit from training workshops that receive weekly workshops on more than 10 different topics. It is also worth highlighting the senior citizen program, which benefits about 50 people over 75 years of age in the community.

As a Center that is committed to environmental education, its heritage values ​​legitimize its Cubanness, contributing to developing cultural and national identity, as well as forming an environmental culture. More than 10 primary and secondary schools are linked to the extracurricular training programs offered by Botanic Garden of Havana "Quinta de los Molinos”, which benefits more than 1,000 children annually.

Sustainability

As a Centre that is committed to environmental education, contributing to the development of an environmental culture, the garden develops environmental workshops with 10 schools in the area, as well as environmental festivals with an average annual participation of 1,000 people. In addition, it uses the facilities of the Renewable Energy Demonstration Centre for training in clean energy issues. This centre also generates 120 % of the energy we consumes from renewable energy sources (we have installed 144 solar panels and three wind turbines).

Botanic Garden of Havana "Quinta de los Molinos” is also the only event organiser nationwide that can manage Zero Emissions events, from energy generation and carbon footprint offsetting with the heritage forest it houses. In this sense, at Quinta de los Molinos the Circular Economy is promoted from the reuse of forest waste and composting.

Last, La Quinta manages Cuba's only Butterfly House as a space for promoting environmental values. On the other hand, the use of wild pets and other positive interactions with animals is promoted, eliminating all caged animals from the park in recent years.
mission_statement:
The Havana Botanic Garden "Quinta de los Molinos", through its Sustainability Program:

  • Promotes being a space for the community and local development;

  • Defends Cultural and Natural Heritage;

  • Guarantees the continuity of social programs;

  • Generates economic autonomy for the organization and well-being for its workers;

  • It consolidates itself as a Reference Center for Labor Insertion;

  • Guarantees its sustainable economic management;

  • Consolidates high standards of social and environmental responsibility;

  • Promotes the use of renewable sources of energy, the circular, social, solidarity and creative economy.

overview_statement:
Established in 1979 at the site of the century old Agricultural Experimental Station, the Joseph Reynold O'Neal Botanic Gardens (JRONBG) are an oasis in the centre of Road Town, Tortola. The gardens, which is also a national park, is named after the BVI's first conservationist, who was also a leading figure in the establishment of the National Parks Trust of the Virgin Islands.

The JRONBG and the National Parks Trust works closely with the Royal Botanic Gardens Kew (Kew) to conduct field research on the BVI's threatened plant species and conserve these in the wild and ex-situ at the JRONBG and Kew.

overview_statement: The James Cook University Living Collection's encompass all flora on campus, from our bush-land to gardens, and indoor plants. The collection is housed across all campuses, and remote sites, with accurate mapping and species surveying in place for our collections management.  Plants held in the collection are a combination of wild field collected specimen not grown anywhere else in the world, rare and threatened species, bush tuckers, traditional use species and generic horticultural species from all over the world.  The living collections are guided through each campuses unique Master Plans, and embrace 7 principals of engagement and representation, these are Education and Research, Connection to Country, Cultural significance,  Conservation, Sustainability, Mental health and Aesthetics.

overview_statement: Dilla University Botanical and Ecotourism Garden (DUBEG) was established in 2017 for conservation, research, education, and recreation. It is located in a strategic ecoregion and floristic region to conserve and manage the plant diversity of Ethiopia. It is located in the transitional altitude (1300-1500) range between lowland and midland, which makes it suitable for conservative both lowland and midland plant diversity. Based on floristic region DUBEG is located in the Sidamo floristic region, which is the most diversified floristic region among the 16 floristic regions of Ethiopia and Eritrea. Generally, DUBEG has significant value in conservatively and manage Ethiopia plant diversity.

overview_statement:
The Greenhouses of the Botanical Garden are an emblematic space situated in Liege, Belgium, dedicated to the conservation and enhancement of the world’s botanical heritage. They house a diverse living collection within a historic and urban setting imbued with poetry, making them a unique place in Wallonia. Driven by a passionate team, the greenhouses aspire to become an innovative model in energy-efficient management and botanical valorization, serving the transmission of knowledge and cultural outreach.

The Greenhouses of the Botanical Garden are also home to a significant chapter in scientific history: it was here that Charles Morren discovered, in 1836, the mechanism of artificial pollination of vanilla—an innovation that revolutionized its cultivation worldwide.
mission_statement:
At the Liège Botanical Garden, our mission is to preserve, enrich, and share the extraordinary diversity of the plant world. As the only historic botanical garden in Wallonia, we strive to be a beacon of knowledge and inspiration, highlighting the essential role of plants in our ecosystems and daily lives.

By continuously expanding and improving our collections, refining their labeling, and maintaining diverse biomes, we offer an immersive educational experience that fosters curiosity and engagement. Our commitment to environmental education (ErE) is reinforced through strong local partnerships and dynamic exchanges with botanical garden networks, including VBTA (Belgium), JBF (France), and BGCI (internationally).

We aspire to develop a high-quality educational program, ensuring that the botanical garden serves as a platform for discovery, scientific learning, and environmental awareness. By integrating an education team, we aim to further enrich our outreach and inspire future generations to appreciate, study, and protect the plant world.

organisation_name: The Gardens of Fanshawe College and the A.M. Cuddy Gardens
Botanical Garden at University Hawaii - Hilo
overview_statement:
The Botanical Garden at UH Hilo is a two-acre, volunteer-driven garden dedicated to the conservation, study, and display of tropical plant diversity, with particular strength in cycads, bromeliads, and palms. Though modest in size, the garden has developed one of Hawaiʻi’s most comprehensive living collections of cycads, making it an important resource for education and plant conservation in the Pacific region.

The cycad collection is the centerpiece of the garden and includes 134 species representing 10 genera from Africa, Asia, Australia, and the Americas. Several accessions represent taxa that remain undescribed or are still being formally named, reflecting the garden’s engagement with ongoing taxonomic research. A particularly notable feature is a dedicated Zamia section containing 49 species from Mexico, Central America, and South America. This grouping highlights the extraordinary diversity within the genus—from species adapted to dry tropical forests to those thriving in humid rainforest understories. Many of these cycads are rare or threatened in the wild, so maintaining them in cultivation supports broader conservation goals and helps educate visitors about the vulnerability of ancient plant lineages.

The garden also maintains a large bromeliad collection composed primarily of hybrids developed by Hilo grower David Shiigi. These plants display an impressive range of leaf color, form, and inflorescence structure, from compact rosettes to dramatic, long-lasting blooms. Many are naturally adapted to grow on trees or in well-drained conditions and are well suited to Hawaiʻi’s climate. The collection provides year-round color and demonstrates how selective breeding can enhance the ornamental qualities of tropical plants while still reflecting their natural diversity.

The palm collection further expands the garden’s global representation. Towering species from the South Pacific, such as Pigafetta elata and Clinostigma samoense, create dramatic vertical structure within the landscape. In contrast, smaller understory palms such as Licuala species from Thailand and Chamaedorea species from Central and South America offer finely textured foliage and adaptability to shaded conditions. Together, these plantings illustrate the remarkable range of form and habitat found within the palm family.

Maintained entirely through private donations and the dedication of approximately ten regular volunteers, the Botanical Garden at UH Hilo operates without direct financial or operational support from the University. Despite its small size, it functions as a living classroom for students, researchers, and the broader community, with a strong emphasis on conservation, horticultural excellence, and the preservation of rare tropical plants.

Last updated 2/27/26
mission_statement: The Botanical Garden at the University of Hawaii at Hilo increases public awareness and appreciation of the plant kingdom and nature itself and fosters greater understanding, appreciation, and stewardship of Earth’s botanical diversity and its essential value to mankind. Aligned with the University's mission, the botanical garden's purpose is to enrich current and upcoming generations by cultivating and sharing the inherent wisdom of the natural world.

organisation_name: The Arboretum at Moses Brown School
overview_statement: The Arboretum at Moses Brown spreads throughout the Friends school’s 43-acre campus on the East Side of Providence, RI. The Arboretum includes many mature trees and shrubs, particularly a variety of stately oaks and beeches; one European beech is among the oldest trees in Providence, according to the Rhode Island Tree Council. Among the younger trees on the campus, forty have been planted in honor of faculty and staff with thirty years or more of service to the school; a variety of memorial trees and gardens are also located around the campus. In line with its mission to “instill the utmost care for learning, people, and place,” the Arboretum provides educational opportunities for its current students, faculty, and staff while also celebrating the rich heritage of the school.
mission_statement:
In line with the school’s mission “to inspire the inner promise of each student and instill the utmost care for learning, people, and place,” the purpose of The Arboretum at Moses Brown is to enhance, maintain, study and celebrate the trees and woody plants on the school’s 43-acre campus.

Objectives:

●  To care for the trees and woody plants currently within the arboretum as well as additional trees planted as part of ongoing campus enhancements.

●  To provide educational and volunteer opportunities for students, faculty and staff throughout the school community.

●  To educate alumni, visitors and those in the nearby community about the benefits, both natural and aesthetic, that trees and woody plants provide people in an urban setting.

●  To celebrate faculty and staff with 30+ years of service to the school

●  To catalogue fully the different species of trees and woody plants on the campus.

Governance: Moses Brown’s Sustainability Committee acts as the governing group for the school’s arboretum. The Sustainability Committee includes faculty members from all three divisions of the school, the student co-clerks of the Upper School Environmental Council, staff members from the Operations Department, including those responsible for maintaining the school’s grounds, and members of the senior administrative staff, including the Head of School. The arboretum also benefits from the expertise of the arborist (from Stanley Tree Service) that the school retains.

mission_statement:
The Centre National de Floristique (CNF) at the Université Félix HOUPHOUËT-BOIGNY, Côte d'Ivoire, is an institute of the Université Félix HOUPHOUËT-BOIGNY dedicated to research and publication. It also ensures the in-situ and ex-situ conservation of Ivorian flora. The center covers an area of 10ha35 and houses a botanical garden and the National Herbarium. Today, it is brimming with immense potential in terms of rich flora and ecosystem services that are still unknown to the Ivorian population. It comprises two major entities:

§ The Living Collection, comprising:

ü A 4.72 ha Arboretum planted in 11 thematic plots.

ü A Fallow land: area of 5.63 ha

According to the latest studies, there are 555 vascular plants in 380 genera and 103 botanical families, and 127 special-status species (Aké-Assi, 1998):

ü 79 endemic species (56 endemic to West Africa, 49 endemic to Upper Guinea, 9 endemic to Côte d'Ivoire)

ü 49 species on the IUCN Red List, 2018 (37 vulnerable, 5 endangered, 3 Least Concern and 4 Near Threatened);

ü 27 species are listed by Aké-Assi, 1998 (26 species rare, becoming rare and/or threatened with extinction and one extinct species: Cola Lorougnonis). Some species have dual status.

The studies also list 265 useful plants:

ü 87 timber species;

ü 183 medicinal species;

ü 30 food species;

ü 34 ornamental species.

§ The Inert Collection composed of:

ü Herbarium (dried plants): 29362 specimens; 18832 occurrences, 4257 plants; 1485 genera; 226 botanical families; 226 medicinal plants.

ü Harvesting period: 1900-2017, enabling us to trace the history of rare and/or endangered species.

ü Origin of Ivorian, West African and exotic plants

The Centre's emblematic species are :

ü 1 extinct species: Cola Lorougnonis ;

ü Rare and vulnerable species: Schumanniophyton problematicum, Milletia regia (Iroko), Milletia excelsa (Iroko) ;

ü 1 rare and endangered species: Pericopsis elata (Assamela) ;

ü 1 rare, endangered and vulnerable species: Garcinia Kola (Petit cola);

ü 1 rare species: Okoubaka aubrevillei ;

ü 1 endangered species: Tieghemella heckelii (Makoré) ;

ü 1 near-threatened species: Irvingia gabonensis (Kaklou);

ü Vulnerable species: Afzelia africana, Albizia adiantifolia, Albizia ferruginea, g. Entandrophragma, g. Khaya (Mahogany), Lophira alata, Nesogordonia papaverifera, Pterygota macrocarpa, Heritiera utilis (Niangon), Terminalia ivorensis (Framiré), Turraeanthus africanus, Khaya senegalensis (Caïlcédrat, Senegal mahogany).

The CNF's missions include :

Ø Carrying out botanical studies (drafting flora, drawing up vegetation maps, plant studies and all floristic inventories);

Ø Carrying out studies on medicinal plants;

Ø Carrying out studies on the protection of flora;

Ø Conservation of the National Herbarium, the statistical and chronological basis of the flora inventory;

Ø Creation of a botanical museum and extension of the garden;

Ø Creation of a library of systematic and taxonomic works.

overview_statement: Park of the Jablunkov Sanatorium is located in the foothills of the Beskids Mountains, at the confluence of the brooks Lomná and Ošetnice. It covers an area of 37,5 hectares. The park was founded in 1924 by the Silesian Humanity association. Its origin and functioning are closely related to the construction and operation of the pulmonary sanatorium. The priority of the park is to help the successful treatment and relaxation of patients. It is also a living collection of many types of plants, it is home to the local fauna. Currently, about 3 000 taxa – woody plants and perennials are cultivated in the park. The plantings are designed in such a way that the visitor is rewarded with the sight of beautiful scenery and colors while walking throughout the year. The water cascade, ponds, gazebos and sculptures give the park a specific atmosphere suitable for relaxation of patients and visitors. An educational trail informs visitors about the history of the park and sanatorium. The park is open to the public. Most footpaths are barrier-free. Since 1975, the park and the sanatorium building have been protected by the legislation of the Czech Republic as a Cultural Monument, since 1994 as an important landscape element. Since 2005, park has been a member of the newly formed Union of Botanical Gardens of the Czech Republic. Since 2023, the genera Stewartia and Acer have been declared the National Collection of the Union of Botanic Gardens.

overview_statement:
This site includes: MUSE living collections and Trentino Seedbank.

MUSE green areas host living botanical collections that fall into three distinct categories of species and projects:

  1. Tropical Collections: these include Afrotropical species housed in the exhibition Conservatory (part of the museum’s tour itinerary) and in the nursery greenhouses. The latter host educational, research, and display collections. Additionally, these greenhouses cultivate plant species used in the museum’s terrariums and aquariums to establish suitable habitats for live animals. The plant material is derived from exchanges with Botanical Gardens participating in the International Plant Exchange Network (IPEN), acquisitions from specialized nurseries, and field collections conducted under research permits at the museum’s Tanzanian field station.

  2. Outdoor Garden Collections: species with ornamental functions and thematic collections (traditional vegetable garden, flora of Continents, rose garden collection, Mediterranean hedge, neglected fruit species and traditional landraces).

  3. Biotope Collection: this collection includes native wetland species of high conservation value and local genotypes, representative of key wetland ecosystems within the Province.

The core of the tropical collections is the exhibition Conservatory, a permanent installation designed to recreate Tanzania’s tropical mountains habitats. Established in 2013, the greenhouse was conceived to illustrate the museum’s activities in tropical montane regions and to more broadly communicate issues of biodiversity and sustainability in tropical ecosystems.

Specifically, the focus is on Tanzania, and more precisely the Udzungwa Mountains, where MUSE maintains a field station at the edge of the Udzungwa Mountains National Park. This station supports ongoing research projects in both ecological and social fields.

Thanks to the museum staff’s expertise in mountain ecosystems and an integrated approach that combines scientific research with public engagement and education, the greenhouse serves as an ideal platform for translating local topics into global narratives. It enhances the museum’s overall visitor experience and contributes to broader discussions on sustainability and biodiversity through a rich program of events and temporary exhibitions.

organisation_name: New England Botanic Garden at Tower Hill
overview_statement:
The Worcester County Horticultural Society, founded in 1842, established New England Botanic Garden at Tower Hill in Boylston, MA as a horticultural resource—a place for people to experience the wonder of plants, learn about the natural world, and make joyful connections. Our doors opened in 1986 and we’ve continued to grow our mission, our footprint, and our role in the community ever since. Today’s Garden sits on 200 acres. It includes conservatories, formal and naturalistic gardens, a café, Garden Shop, walking trails, accessible pathways, and expansive views of the Wachusett Reservoir. A nonprofit organization and AAM-accredited museum, we care for an irreplaceable collection of plants and place sustainability and environmental stewardship at the forefront of our work. A robust, year-round calendar of educational classes, activities, and events engages people of all ages in meaningful experiences with plants.  

We’re proud to be a garden where everyone belongs, where wandering is always welcome, and where no two visits will ever be quite the same.

organisation_name_alt: อุทยานหลวงราชพฤกษ์
overview_statement:
In 2006 the Royal Thai Government, through the Department of Agriculture, under the Ministry of Agriculture and Cooperatives organized the International Horticultural Exposition at the Royal Agricultural Research Centre, Chiang Mai, for His Majesty King Bhumibol Adulyadej of Thailand in celebration of the 60th Anniversary of His Majesty’s Accession to the Throne and His 80th Birthday Anniversary.

The exposition was extremely successful. There were a total of more than 3 million visitors including foreigners visited the Exposition.

In 2008, the Cabinet, in order to extend the success of the exposition and to make use of the International Horticultural Exposition area for maximum benefit, has authorized the Highland Research and Development Institute (Public Organization) to manage the area since December 11, 2009 as a learning centre for botanical agriculture and the site for agro-tourism and culture at the international level of Thailand.

Subsequently, His Majesty the King has graciously given the name of this area as “The Royal Park Rajapruek” since January 23, 2010.
mission_statement:
Our Goal

Our aim is achieve that Highland people live with a sufficient income along with a better livelihood which is generated from a more environmental friendly agriculture production and a strengthened community.

Vision

- To ensure socially and environmentally sustainable highland development supporting the Royal Project’s research and development efforts and extending them to highland communities throughout the country and further, including those that Royal project activities have not previously reached.

- To develop the Royal Park Rajapruek as an internationally recognized hub of horticultural and cultural knowledge, biodiversity and high quality eco-tourism.

Objectives

1. To extend and support the research and development activities of the Royal Project.

2. To support conservation and sustainable utilization of the biodiversity inherent to the Thai highlands by researching, recording, conserving and developing local knowledge.

3. To support and work with the Royal Project Foundation and related agencies in strengthening highland communities and environmental education ensuring sustainable co-existence with the environment that is in line with the philosophy of a sufficient economy.

4. To investigate, research and disseminate data and information related to highland development and to act as a research and extension coordination center.

5. To build up cooperative networks, both domestically and internationally, to exchange best practice research and development in the highlands.

6. To establish the Royal Park Rajapruek as a learning center of excellence in horticulture and biodiversity and as a tourist attraction for agriculture and culture.

The Paradigm of Sustainable Highland Development

organisation_name_alt: Jardim Botânico da Universidade do Porto
overview_statement:
The Botanical Garden of the University of Porto is part of the second pole of the MHNC-UP, located in the old Quinta do Campo Alegre in Porto. It is a garden of great botanical, historical, artistic and literary interest, in which the interventions of the late 19th century and the second half of the 20th century stand out and whose history evokes important figures of 20th century Portuguese literature – Sophia de Mello Breyner Andresen and Ruben A. The garden houses the Hall of Biodiversity – Ciência Viva Center, a space dedicated to the promotion of scientific culture in the scope of the biological sciences, evolution and biodiversity; and Casa Salabert, which harbours U.Porto’s E-Learning Café – Botânico.

It is organized in three levels with very different characteristics. On the first level, there are the entrance bosquets, the Hall of Biodiversity – Centro Ciência Viva, surrounded by a mixed border of native species, and the formal gardens, compartmentalised by tall hedges of centenary camellias: the Garden of Jotas, the Rose Garden, the Bronze Boy Garden, the Schist Garden, the Fish Garden, the Dwarf Garden and the Liquidambar Garden. On the second level are the Cactus and Succulent Garden and the greenhouses. The third, and lowest, level houses the Arboretum, the little reservoir and the large lake.

overview_statement:
The history of the Royal Botanic Gardens dates as far back as 1371 when King Wickramabahu III ascended the thrown and kept court at Peradeniya near Mahaweli river. Later, in the reign of King Kirti Sri from 1747 - 1780 King Rajadhi Rajasinghe resided therein, where a temporary residence was erected for him.

A vihare and dagaba were built in the reign of King Wimala Dhamma which was improved by Kind Rajadhi Rajasinghe. The vihare and dogaba were destroyed by the English when they occupied Kandy. The famous historical battle of Gannoruwa between Rajasinghe II and the Portuguese was fought on the Northern side of the river. A priest resided here till the Gardens were formed by Mr Alexandar Moon in 1821 six years after the final conquest of the Kandyan Kingdom.

In 1810 under the advice of Sir Joseph Banks a garden named Kew was opened in Slave island and Mr William Kerr was appointed as its Superintendent. In 1813 the garden was moved to Kalutara for the reception of economic plants which could be cultivated there on a larger scale than was possible at Slave island. Kerr died in 1814 and under the rule of his successor Mr Alexander Moon this Garden was finally moved to Peradeniya in 1821 as it was found to be favorable and better adapted for the proposed Botanic establishment. The transfer of exotics from the Kalutara Garden was made by successive Superintendents at least up to 1843.

During Moon's superintendent the opening of the Royal Botanic Gardens, Peradeniya, can be said to have commenced though at first only the South West portion of the Gardens was cleared and opened and it was mostly planted with cinnamon and coffee. Moon published his "Catalogue of Ceylon Plants" in 1824 in which was given the Botanical and native names of 1, 127 plants, indigenous to the island. After the appointment of Mr George Gardner in 1844 the institution started upon its more active independent and useful existence that it has since maintained. Only 40 acres of the 147 acres were in cultivation when Gardener took charge and the chief use made of the land was to grow jak, coconuts and vegetables for sale by the Government Agent in Kandy. Gardner effected many important improvements in the condition of the Gardens but his chief work was the exploration of the country for the collection and preparation of its flora. He died at Nuwara Eliya in 1849 and was succeeded by Dr Thwaites who for over 30 years maintained the Gardens in a high state of efficiency, added largely to our knowledge of the flora of the Colony and gave the establishment its worldwide reputation. Botanic Gardens at Hakgala was established in 1861 for introduction of Cinchona into the island and in 1876 Gampaha (Henarathgoda) Botanic Garden was started for the introduction of Rubber.

Thwaites was succeeded by Dr Henry Trimen, under whose rule and capable management the beauty and usefulness of the Gardens were very considerably advanced. He established the Museum of Economic Botany, opened branch Gardens at Badulla and Anuradhapura and began the publication of his work, "The Flora of Ceylon" which however was finished by Sir Joseph D. Hooker after Trimen's death in 1896. In 1896 Trimen was succeeded by Dr J.C. Willis and from that date a new extension of scientific work took place. In the early years work was mainly directed towards the introduction and acclimatization of useful and ornamental plants but in later years activities developed towards Economic, Botany and Agriculture and led to the development of the Department of Agriculture in 1912. Mr H.F. Macmillan who was appointed Curator in 1895, was made the Superintendent of Botanic Gardens in 1912 and Mr T.H. Parsons the Curator in 1914. During Macmillan's superintendent the Gardens were improved and extended and his great work "a Hand Book of Tropical Planting and Gardening" was published. Macmillan retired in 1925 and Mr T.H. Parsons continued as curator till 1945.

organisation_name: Taman Botani Negara Shah Alam/ National Botanic Gardens Shah Alam
overview_statement:
The National Botanical Garden Shah Alam (TBNSA) previously known as Taman Pertanian Malaysia (TPM) and initially known as Bukit Cerakah Agriculture Park was developed on 24th April 1986 before it was promulgated as the Bukit Cahaya Seri Alam Agriculture Park Malaysia by the late Almarhum Sultan Salahuddin Abdul Aziz Shah Al-Haj ibni Hishamuddin Alam Shah Al-Haj in 1991. The name TBNSA conferred to the park is in line with the decision made by the Cabinet of Ministers in 2007 to further develop TBNSA as a replacement to TPM.  

National Botanic Gardens Shah Alam, is centrally located within Klang Valley. It is at the fringe of the urban area of Shah Alam namely at Section U11 and strategically within 20 kilometers radius of other population catchment areas of Klang, Subang Jaya, Petaling Jaya, Sungai Buluh And Kuala Lumpur. The site covers an area of about 817 hectares with undulating terrain ranging from 18 meters to 220 meters above sea level. The highest point is at Puncak Bukit Sapu Tangan located on the north west corner of the site which provides a clear view of Shah Alarn City Area.

The temperature is consistently high throughout the year. The 24-hr mean temperature fluctuated within a small range from 27°C to 29°C. Although the values may vary from year to year, temperature is slightly higher during the drier Southwest Monsoonal period and lower in October to December when rainfall is higher. The mean maximum temperature fluctuated from 32°C to 34°C while the minimum temperature remained fairly constant at around 24°C to 25°C throughout the year.
mission_statement:
Development of Taman Botani Negara Shah Alam is to serve as a national scientific, education and conservation resource center for development of botany, horticulture, floriculture, agriculture and various other related fields in Malaysia. The intention is also to inspire public awareness on the fields whilst providing public enjoyment of our Malaysian plant heritage.

  • To document, protect and promote conservation of native flora of Malaysia especially the rare, vulnerable and valuable plants of our tropical forest;

  • To educate and create public awareness on the role of plants and forest as part of the ecosystem;

  • To develop a sense of appreciation on the richness of plant species available in the country;

  • To provide a pleasant recreational opportunities to the community within the scope of natural environment.

organisation_name: University of Nevada, Reno Extension Botanic Gardens Las Vegas
overview_statement: Extension's seven-acre outdoor educational Botanic Gardens surround the Extension office at 8050 Paradise Road in Las Vegas. Botanic Gardens are defined by Botanic Garden Conservation International as institutions holding documented collections of living plants for the purpose of scientific research, conservation, display, and education. The Extension Botanic Garden Plant Collection has been curated and designed to tolerate the xeric conditions of southern Nevada. All plant selections and garden designs are water-smart in accordance with SNWA restrictions. Many activities take place in the gardens, including research and volunteer activities. The Botanic Garden Plant Collection contains over 4,500 plants, many of which are subjects of long-term observational studies. The Collection spans the Demonstration and Test Gardens, Pine Grove, The Cactus Garden, the Courtyard Gardens, the Dry Wash, and the Front Gardens. The gardens are open to the public Monday through Friday, from 8 a.m. to 4 p.m. for self-guided tours and guided tours with Master Gardener docents. Call the Botanic Garden Manager, Lauren McGue, at 702-940-5432 for guided tour information or if you have any questions regarding the Collection.
mission_statement: The mission of the Extension Botanic Gardens is to exemplify the highest standards of desert gardening through artistic plant curation, thoughtful landscape design, and water-smart irrigation. All plant selections and designs are water-smart in accordance with SNWA restrictions. As defined by BGCI, botanic gardens are institutions holding documented collections of living plants for the purpose of scientific research, conservation, display, and education. The mission of the Extension Botanic Gardens is executed through the curation and cultivation of our outdoor Plant Collection, which is spread over our seven acres in specialized areas, demonstrations, research areas, groves, and ornamental display areas.

organisation_name: Düzce University Ornamental and Medicinal Plants Botanical Garden (DUSTBB)
organisation_name_alt: Düzce Üniversitesi Süs ve Tıbbi Bitkiler Botanik Bahçesi (DÜSTBB)
overview_statement:
Düzce University Ornamental and Medicinal Plants Botanical Garden /(Düzce Üniversitesi Süs ve Tıbbi Bitkiler Botanik Bahçesi (DÜSTBB) ), located within the borders of Düzce University, is a valley with a total green area of 38293 m², with an area of approximately 51,450 m² and a rickety water flowing under it. The Botanical Garden is a rectangular area extending from north-northeast to south-southwest axis and is surrounded by internal roads.

https://botanikbahce.duzce.edu.tr/

https://w3.api.duzce.edu.tr/akademik/merkez/dustibam
mission_statement:
Düzce University Ornamental and Medicinal Plants Botanical Garden is a living nature museum built on 43 main areas consisting of terraced gardens, rock gardens, waterfalls, streams, pond ecological systems, amphitheatre, nature and botanical museum education systems, collections and garden exhibitions where biomes living on earth are defined: arboretum and recreation area, medicinal aromatic plants garden, Ex-situ Düzce plants, Central Anatolian steppe plants, rock garden, Mediterranean plants, herbaceous-woody plants, geophyte garden, exotic species, pond and aquatic plants, moist stream vegetation, welcome gardens and plant collections.

One of the most important aims and features of Botanical Gardens is to protect endemic and rare plants and to carry out scientific studies on them.  Düzce University Ornamental and Medicinal Plants Botanical Garden (DÜSTBB) was established to play an important role in the conservation of plant biodiversity both in the country and in the region. Ex-situ conservation is aimed in the botanical garden since the habitats of endemic and rare plant taxa in the Western Black Sea Region and Düzce province are threatened by anthropogenic effects. According to the flora, vegetation and monitoring studies carried out in Düzce province and the Western Black Sea Region, there are 11800 plant taxa in the DUOF herbarium and these are also recorded in the virtual herbarium.

In Düzce province, 1255 vascular plant taxa are distributed and 59 of them are endemic and 24 of them are rare plants. According to Flora of Turkey, there are 137 endemic plant taxa in the Western Black Sea Region (Aksoy et al., 2019). Endemic plant habitat areas are under threat and extinction due to anthropogenic factors such as intensive forestry activities, dam construction, stone mining and unplanned tourism activities. In Düzce province, 10 endemic plant taxa [CR (5), EN (2), VU (3)] are under threat. Ex-situ conservation activities are carried out in the botanical garden for local endemic plant taxa Cephalaria duzceensis, Centaurea yaltirikii, Jurinea efeae and Lythrum anatolicum subsp. anatolicum.

overview_statement: Known as Loki Schmidt Garten

For almost 100 years, Rockway Gardens has been a source of horticultural inspiration and beauty for the City of Kitchener in Ontario, Canada. It has been run by the Kitchener Horticultural Society since it was first established in 1928. The Gardens span over 7 acres with a number of different areas of interest. It is most famously known for its stunning and diverse rock gardens, "The Rockery", first developed in 1933. There are many formal Annual Display beds that also include an Annual Trial Garden Area. There are six water features on the property including two pond systems integrated into the Rockery. Other areas of interest would be a perennial border, the tree collection, the Native Woodland Hillside and the Native Meadow.

overview_statement:
El Jardín Etnobiológico Tachi’í de Nayarit se localiza en el valle de Matatipac rodeado de antiguos volcanes boscosos que dan vida a un gran numero de manantiales, ofreciendo abundante agua para el desarrollo de la biodiversidad en la zona, así como para satisfacer los servicios de la capital del Estado. En la parte más baja de este valle se localizan una serie de humedales que resguardan y alimentan los mantos freáticos de la zona, regulando además las crecientes del Río Mololoa, principal caudal que atraviesa la ciudad.

 

Dentro de este complejo paisaje e inmerso en la creciente mancha urbana de la capital del Estado, habita el Jardín Etnobiológico Tachí’i dentro de una reserva natural protegida de competencia municipal denominada Parque Ecológico Tachí’i, compuesta por 25 hectáreas de zonas inundables y densamente arboladas en igual proporción que puede variar entre la temporada de lluvias y estiaje.

 

El Jardín cuenta con diversos servicios para el uso y disfrute de sus visitantes en equilibrio con los organismos residentes y migratorios, compuestos por áreas verdes, trotapista, ciclopista, área de juegos, baños, oficinas, así como una unidad de manejo para la conservación de la vida silvestre, lo anterior se suma a las nuevas áreas incorporadas a través del proyecto de la RENAJEB que promueve la CONAHCYT, entre las que destacan, una sala de educación ambiental que integra el repositorio físico del proyecto, colecciones vivas de plantas , vivero de planta nativa, así como banco de semillas y próximos espacios como el Jardín Etnofamacologico y el centro de artesanos Takie como parte de la colaboración y visibilización del pueblo Wixárika en el proyecto y el reconocimiento de sus saberes asociados a la biodiversidad en el estado.

overview_statement:
The Orchidarium and Botanical Garden (OJBC) is currently developing the project “Rescue and exhibition of the flora of the Meseta Comiteca Tojolabal Region” whose main objective is the ex situ and in situ conservation of plant genetic resources, the control of the destruction of plant biodiversity and environmental education. It also generates links with institutions, civil society and international organizations under the purpose of environmental development.

The OJBC has a database with 456 records of plant species, corresponding to 2,154 specimens of 246 genera and 80 families. Of these, 226 are native and 55 are exotic. The most representative families are Orchidaceae and Bromeliaceae, which represent 38% and 7% of the living collection. The most diverse genera are Tillandsia and Prosthechea. Existing collections are also being enriched and new collections of charismatic plants such as begonias, heliconias and aquatic plants are being formed (Martínez-Meléndez et al. 2024). This living collection is maintained by five gardeners, three biologists who manage plants in greenhouses and a general curator.

The data of the herbarium collection can be reviewed in Index herbariorum as OJBC.

overview_statement:
Gathering Place is a world-class riverfront park in Tulsa, Oklahoma, designed to welcome everyone into a vibrant, inclusive community space that inspires, educates, and excites visitors of all ages. Spanning 66.5 acres along the Arkansas River, the park was named USA TODAY’s Best City Park of 2024 and recognized by National Geographic as one of the Top 100 Unexpected Travel Destinations. 

This dynamic green space offers endless opportunities to play, learn, explore, and connect—all at no cost—making it a true destination for Tulsans and visitors from around the world. From a five-acre adventure playground and sports courts to a BMX pump track, meadows, and gardens, the park invites boundless outdoor exploration. 

At the heart of Gathering Place are two iconic buildings designed for discovery: Williams Lodge, a warm and welcoming space to relax and unwind, and the ONEOK Boathouse, a cultural hub featuring permanent and rotating exhibits, as well as a variety of weekly programs. 

The park’s landscape is as impressive as its amenities. With 1.2 million plants representing 400 species, more than 6,000 trees, and 16 acres of native prairie, Gathering Place offers a lush, immersive environment. All of Oklahoma’s ecological regions—from prairies and wetlands to woodlands—are thoughtfully represented, creating an experience that’s as educational as it is breathtaking. 

Every element of Gathering Place is designed to spark joy, curiosity, and connection—making it not just a park, but a place where everyone belongs.
mission_statement: Gathering Place is a world-class riverfront park designed to welcome all Tulsans to a vibrant and inclusive community space that engages, educates, and excites!

overview_statement:
The Jardin des Plantes opened in 1948. Originally bigger than it is now, today it spreads across 11 hectares. It is an ornamental garden that is primarily visited by local residents, particularly during low season and is looking to obtain the official accreditation as a botanical garden from the JBF.

It is composed of a park with wooded areas which harbors 4 main plant collections: a rose garden that surrounds extensive ponds that mainly recreate local wet habitats, a dahlia collection and an area originally dedicated to the study of plant systematics.

Finally, the last area of the garden is composed of different greenhouses : a  horticultural production division that produces all annual and bi-annual plants for the garden and the city at large, and a decoration/greenhouse collection division that looks after the collections which are not frost-resistant, including 2 greenhouses open to the public, one showcasing arid areas and the other tropical wet habitats.

organisation_name: Brooklyn Greenway Initiative’s Naval Cemetery Landscape
overview_statement: Brooklyn Greenway Initiative built and maintains the Naval Cemetery Landscape (NCL) on the site of the former Naval Hospital Cemetery at the Brooklyn Navy Yard as a place for retreat and remembrance while honoring its rich layers of natural and cultural history. This site was designed as a native plant meadow and pollinator habitat, and many rare birds and insects can be seen here. With self-guided activities and free programs, visitors can learn about native plants, bees and insects and visitors are encouraged to bring their own binoculars to observe the bird species from the boardwalk. NCL’s primary function is as a quiet contemplative memorial landscape where Brooklyn Greenway Initiative (BGI) showcases and champions the potential impact of the Green in Greenways (cyclist and pedestrian corridors that ideally include separation from car lanes and green corridors of street trees, native plantings or both) and provides public programming that enhances connections to nature. The landscape is a connector and place of respite and grounding for community members and users of the adjacent Brooklyn Waterfront Greenway. We strive to limit disruptions to both visitors and land (as a cemetery) and to wildlife (as a native pollinator habitat) and our programs are aimed at building skill sets for urban visitors with an emphasis on nature education and mental wellness activities emphasizing nature connection and observation. The NCL is unique as a cemetery and pollinator habitat, and also as a landscape built, maintained and operated solely by the non-profit Brooklyn Greenway Initiative. Donations support our work at the landscape and our work advocating for the construction and maintenance of safe greenways.
mission_statement:
Brooklyn Greenway Initiative (BGI) is working to build the Brooklyn Waterfront Greenway and expand greenways in NYC. BGI is committed to the establishment, development and long-term stewardship of the Brooklyn Waterfront Greenway. Founded in 2004, BGI works with community, business, and governmental partners to create and fulfill a comprehensive vision for the Greenway.

For over a 20 years Brooklyn Greenway Initiative (BGI) has acted as the catalyst for the development, establishment and long-term stewardship of the Brooklyn Waterfront Greenway, a 29-mile protected and landscaped route for pedestrians and cyclists (and wildlife!). The Naval Cemetery Landscape showcases how well-designed, well-maintained native plant communities and conservation education along the greenways will benefit the everyone when included in greenway planning.

overview_statement:
El Jardín Botánico Quilapilún fue inaugurado en 2012 como una iniciativa de Anglo American para promover el conocimiento y la valoración de la biodiversidad chilena, en especial del ecosistema mediterráneo de la zona central. Concebido como un espacio de educación, conservación y recreación, el parque alberga la primera colección botánica dedicada exclusivamente a la flora nativa y endémica de la Región Metropolitana de Santiago.

A lo largo de su trayectoria, el parque ha desarrollado programas educativos, actividades culturales y líneas de base ecológicas que han permitido profundizar su rol como plataforma de encuentro entre las personas y la naturaleza. Su diseño paisajístico, infraestructura y diversidad vegetal lo han posicionado como un referente regional en la divulgación de la flora nativa.

A través de objetivos definidos, acciones priorizadas y un enfoque basado en buenas prácticas, el parque busca fortalecer su contribución a la conservación vegetal, a la educación ambiental y a la sostenibilidad institucional.
mission_statement: Proporcionar un espacio accessible para la investigación, la conservación y la educación ambiental que fomente la conexión entre las personas y la naturaleza, valorando la flora nativa del ecosistema mediterráneo chileno mediante la conservación, la divulgación del conocimiento botánico y la participación comunitaria.

overview_statement: La Constancia de Biocca is a developing botanical garden and arboretum located in the city of Mar del Plata, Buenos Aires Province, Argentina. Established on the grounds of a historic family estate, its mission is to conserve plant biodiversity, promote environmental education, and strengthen the connection between people and nature. The site is home to more than 300 plant species and over 40 bird species, offering a rich environment for ecological learning and biodiversity appreciation. Through school visits, educational programmes, and nature-based well-being activities such as forest therapy, La Constancia de Biocca aims to become a reference point for science communication, landscape conservation, and community wellness.
mission_statement: La Constancia de Biocca is dedicated to the conservation of plant biodiversity, the promotion of environmental education, and the cultivation of a deeper connection between people and nature. Through the development of its botanical collections, educational initiatives and nature-based well-being activities, La Constancia de Biocca seeks to inspire ecological awareness, support scientific learning, foster holistic wellness, and preserve the natural and cultural heritage for future generations.

overview_statement:
El Jardín Botánico La Macarena es una reserva para mantener, proteger y estudiar la fauna y flora existente. El estudio científico de la flora en la reserva muestra la presencia de más de 1175 especies nativas, es decir presentes sin hacer nada, lo que equivale a más del 4 por ciento de la biodiversidad colombiana. Afuera de eso hay más de 200 otras especies.

Si aún existe la presencia de una hacienda ganadera como práctica de convivencia más amigable con el medio ambiente, es para demostrar que es posible mitigar el impacto del ganado y beneficiarse de su presencia para desarrollar fertilizantes con microbiología local para jardines con productos biológicos.

The La Macarena Botanical Garden is a reserve dedicated to maintaining, protecting, and studying the existing fauna and flora. Scientific studies of the flora within the reserve show the presence of more than 1,175 native species, meaning those present without human intervention, which amounts to over 4 per cent of Colombia's biodiversity. In addition, there are more than 200 other species.

If a cattle ranch still exists as a more environmentally friendly practice of coexistence, it is to demonstrate that it is possible to mitigate the impact of livestock and to benefit from their presence by developing fertilisers with local microbiology for gardens using biological products.

overview_statement:
DISCOVERY GARDENS

Visit our Discovery Gardens and see how you can implement Florida-Friendly Landscaping™ in your backyard with beautiful results. 28 themed gardens in a 3.5-acre garden provide a variety of plants and themes to consider for your garden. Discovery Gardens is open to the public Monday - Friday 9:00 am - 4:00 pm, and now open Saturdays from 9:00 am - 3:00 pm. You can take an audio tour using a QR code located on the large map under the green arbor at the entrance. A guided tour can be scheduled by contacting Maria Bautista at mquiricobautista@ufl.edu or completing and sending the form: Discovery Gardens Tour Request Form
mission_statement:
The Mission of the Discovery Gardens

  • To support the educational mission of the Lake County Extension by creating an exemplary garden facility for hands-on-training

  • To create an outstanding visitor attraction - -a well-designed botanical garden

  • To promote conservation of natural resources by demonstrating environmentally friendly practices for gardening and landscaping

  • To provide a focal point for all local groups and individuals interested in horticulture

  • Lake County's Discovery Gardens are an educational resource developed to support programs in horticulture, gardening, landscape design and natural resource management.

Programs are offered for homeowners, garden enthusiasts, educators, children and the horticulture industry.  There are self-guided tours assisted with brochures and plant labeling.  So, follow along as we explore each of the garden areas.

First, a little about the Discovery Garden.  The Discovery Gardens are located at the UF/IFAS Lake County Extension Center, 1951 Woodlea Road, Tavares, Florida 32778-4262.  It is situated on a 3 1/2-acre site made up of 28 major theme gardens, each designed to show a different gardening aspect in Central Florida.  It has more than 700 different plants and is dedicated to demonstrating how homeowners can accomplish the landscape they want. All plants are labeled, and cultural information is available upon request at the Master Gardener Plant Clinic in the main building.

If you, your garden club, or group would like a guided tour of the Discovery Gardens please complete the Discovery Gardens Tour Request Form and return the completed form to Maria Bautista at mquiricobautista@ufl.edu

overview_statement:
The 'Hofi Shon Shoco' Native Plant Botanic Garden is a tiny, freely accessible botanic garden located in Parke Nacional Arikok, Aruba (Dutch Caribbean). It currently serves as an educational and recreational area with native flora, benches, signage, a mock historic adobe house, and a small greenhouse.

In 2026, a redesign and expansion of the native plant botanic garden will be initiated to transform it into an urban-scale, regionally unique botanic garden, integrating science, conservation, education, recreation and sustainability. This unique native plant botanic garden will function as an inspirational sanctuary that educates visitors—both locals and tourists—on the importance of native plant gardening to support biodiversity, sustainability, and climate resilience. This living exhibit will serve as a model for how Arubans can integrate native plants into their home gardens and landscaping to conserve water, attract pollinators, support native biodiversity and promote ecological balance.
mission_statement:
“Where Native Plants Inspire a Greener Tomorrow.”

Hofi Shon Shoco is dedicated to advancing the science and practice of native plant conservation. Through research, education, and sustainable practices, we aim to restore biodiversity, enhance climate resilience, and promote ecological balance across Aruba. By showcasing the vital role of native flora in healthy ecosystems, we inspire communities to adopt biodiversity-based gardening practices for a greener, more sustainable future.

overview_statement: The Wild Garden at Meda Gedara is an ambitious project to restore an area of coastal forest, and to create a living classroom to demonstrate the importance of biodiversity to the community and the wider environment.
mission_statement: The Meda Gedara Wild Garden exists to enhance biodiversity through the conservation of native and rare plants, the restoration of habitats, and the support of local wildlife. As a living classroom for both children and adults, it provides opportunities to learn about biodiversity, ecological relationships, and the importance of protecting the natural environment. Through this approach, the garden aims to demonstrate that tourism can create lasting benefits for both the local community and the surrounding environment.

overview_statement:
Award-winning Korean garden destination where the spirit of Jeju truly lives

Since 1968, Spirited Garden has been meticulously developed by farmer Sung Bum-Yung, who transformed barren land in Jeoji-ri, Hangyeong-myeon, Jeju, into a 43,000㎡ estate with eight distinct gardens. The garden features traditional Korean trees, bonsai, unusual stones, and viewing stones, all arranged across the Grass Square and volcanic peaks. Massive hand-crafted volcanic stones, stone walls, and a stone gate, along with cascading waterfalls and ponds, harmonize with natural stone structures, showcasing the unique beauty of Korean gardens and reflecting Jeju’s natural elegance.

Spirited Garden is the only South Korean garden introduced among the world’s top 60 gardens and stands as Jeju’s premier state guest destination. With its growing international recognition as a "world-class garden," it continues to promote Korean garden culture worldwide and has gained renewed attention as the venue for the APEC Jeju Summit.
mission_statement:
In 1968, Sung Bum-Young began transforming barren land , marking the beginning of an extraordinary journey

  When he created something unprecedented in an overlooked, thorny wilderness, many Koreans dismissed bonsai and gardens as merely part of Japanese culture. 

Later, when three Chinese presidents and numerous influential leaders visited, and when Spirited Garden was introduced in Chinese textbooks, people questioned its connection to China. 

 Spirited Garden remains the only Korean garden featured in globally renowned gardening books from the UK and the US. It is also a place where half of the visitors come from Western countries—something that Koreans have found difficult to accept. 

 There has never been a world-class garden created by a single individual in their lifetime. Most prestigious gardens around the world have histories spanning hundreds of years. 

 The fact that South Korea was able to elevate its cultural and artistic identity globally through garden culture was made possible by a pioneer who dedicated 60 years to this vision.
